course.title: How the Body Works
course.description: How the body's main systems work and how they fit together, from cells and tissues to the heart, lungs, gut, kidneys, nerves, hormones and the immune system. Each lesson pairs a mechanism with a practical health link, such as what a blood pressure reading means or how a vaccine works, and none of it is personal medical advice.
course.audience: A curious adult with no biology since school who wants to understand what their own body is doing and to read health information with confidence. They need everyday arithmetic and nothing else. The course does not diagnose, treat or advise any individual, and it does not replace a conversation with a doctor, nurse or pharmacist.

paragraphs: How the body's main systems work and how they fit together, from cells and tissues to the heart, lungs, gut, kidneys, nerves, hormones and the immune system. Each lesson pairs a mechanism with a practical health link, such as what a blood pressure reading means or how a vaccine works, and none of it is personal medical advice.
outcomes: You'll be able to name the four basic tissues and say how one fertilised egg gives rise to many kinds of cell.
You'll be able to explain homeostasis and trace a negative feedback loop for temperature and for blood pressure.
You'll be able to follow blood through the heart and calculate cardiac output from heart rate and stroke volume.
You'll be able to read a blood pressure as systolic over diastolic and say why one reading is not a diagnosis.
You'll be able to explain how air moves in and out, how oxygen reaches the blood, and how to read a respiratory rate against the normal ranges.
You'll be able to follow food through the alimentary canal and work out an energy budget and the WHO's sugar and salt limits.
introduction.prerequisites: No earlier Discere course is needed.

modules.title: Building blocks and balance
modules.description: Cells, tissues, the idea of a steady internal state, and the bones and muscles that show how use shapes tissue.

modules.title: Circulation, breathing and digestion
modules.description: How blood is pumped and measured, how air and food are taken in, and how oxygen and nutrients reach the blood.

modules.title: Energy, balance and control
modules.description: How food becomes energy, how the kidneys, nerves and hormones keep the body steady, and how the immune system and vaccines protect it.

concepts.title: Differentiation
concepts.summary: Early, unspecialised cells become specialised in structure and function as the body develops from a single fertilised egg.

concepts.title: Tissue
concepts.summary: Cells of one kind or a few kinds organised into layers that do one job; the body has four broad categories: epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous.

concepts.title: Stem cell
concepts.summary: An unspecialised cell that can divide without limit as needed and can, under specific conditions, differentiate into specialised cells.

concepts.title: Cell cycle control
concepts.summary: Internal and external stop and advance signals decide when a cell divides; loss of that control can lead to cancer.

concepts.title: Homeostasis
concepts.summary: A dynamic state of balance within parameters that are compatible with life.

concepts.title: Negative feedback
concepts.summary: A response that opposes the change that set it off, so a value is held within a narrow range.

concepts.title: Positive feedback
concepts.summary: A response that adds to the change that set it off, as with oxytocin and labour contractions.

concepts.title: Baroreceptor reflex
concepts.summary: Stretch receptors report blood pressure to the cardiovascular centre, which adjusts the heart and vessels to bring it back.

concepts.title: Bone remodelling
concepts.summary: Osteoblasts form new bone while osteoclasts break down old bone, and the balance between them constantly reshapes it.

concepts.title: Osteoporosis
concepts.summary: A decrease in bone mass that occurs when the rate of bone resorption exceeds the rate of bone formation.

concepts.title: Muscle contraction
concepts.summary: In skeletal and cardiac muscle, myosin pulls on actin once calcium ions expose binding sites, and the process needs ATP.

concepts.title: Hypertrophy and atrophy
concepts.summary: More sarcomeres and myofibrils in each fibre with training, or fewer with disuse; the number of fibres does not change.

concepts.title: Relative risk
concepts.summary: A statement such as a 20 to 30 percent increased risk compares one group with another and is not a count of deaths.

concepts.title: Four chambers
concepts.summary: Two upper receiving chambers, the atria, and two lower pumping chambers, the ventricles, one pair on each side.

concepts.title: Pulmonary and systemic circuits
concepts.summary: The pulmonary circuit takes blood to and from the lungs; the systemic circuit takes oxygenated blood to the tissues and returns it.

concepts.title: Cardiac output
concepts.summary: The amount of blood pumped by each ventricle in one minute: stroke volume multiplied by heart rate.

concepts.title: Resting heart rate
concepts.summary: 60 to 100 beats per minute for a normal adult; below 60 is bradycardia and above 100 is tachycardia.

concepts.title: Blood
concepts.summary: A connective tissue with formed elements (red cells, white cells, platelets) suspended in the fluid plasma.

concepts.title: Arteries, capillaries and veins
concepts.summary: Arteries carry blood away from the heart, capillaries exchange nutrients and wastes, and veins return blood to the heart.

concepts.title: Systolic and diastolic pressure
concepts.summary: The higher number is the pressure when the ventricles contract; the lower is the pressure when they relax.

concepts.title: High blood pressure
concepts.summary: Pressure in the blood vessels that stays too high; it usually causes no symptoms and is found only by measuring.

concepts.title: Respiratory membrane
concepts.summary: The alveolar wall and the capillary wall together, about 0.5 micrometres thick, across which gases pass by simple diffusion.

concepts.title: Pulmonary ventilation
concepts.summary: Movement of air into and out of the lungs, driven by pressure differences made by the diaphragm and the muscles between the ribs.

concepts.title: Passive expiration
concepts.summary: Normal breathing out needs no muscular energy; the lungs recoil as the muscles relax.

concepts.title: Respiratory rate
concepts.summary: Breaths per minute; 12 to 18 for an adolescent or adult, and higher in young children.

concepts.title: Alimentary canal
concepts.summary: A one-way tube from the mouth to the anus, modified as the pharynx, esophagus, stomach and the small and large intestines.

concepts.title: Propulsion and peristalsis
concepts.summary: Swallowing is voluntary; peristalsis is the involuntary sequence of alternating waves of contraction and relaxation that moves food along and mixes it.

concepts.title: Absorption
concepts.summary: Broken-down nutrients pass from the canal into the bloodstream or, for lipids, into lacteals, mainly in the small intestine.

concepts.title: Folds, villi and microvilli
concepts.summary: Three features of the lining that increase the absorptive surface of the small intestine more than 600-fold.

concepts.title: Lactase
concepts.summary: The enzyme that digests the milk sugar lactose; too little of it leads to lactose intolerance.

concepts.title: ATP from glucose
concepts.summary: Glucose from digested carbohydrate is taken up by cells in response to insulin and broken down by glycolysis to make ATP.

concepts.title: Basal metabolic rate
concepts.summary: The daily energy used at rest; about 70 percent of daily expenditure goes to basic organ functions, 20 percent to physical activity and 10 percent to temperature control.

concepts.title: Nutritional Calorie
concepts.summary: The heat needed to raise 1 kg of water by 1 degree Celsius, which differs from the physics calorie.

concepts.title: Four principles of a healthy diet
concepts.summary: Adequacy, balance, moderation and diversity (WHO).

concepts.title: Nephron
concepts.summary: One of about a million tiny structures in each kidney that filter the blood, removing wastes and extra water as urine.

concepts.title: Glomerular filtration rate
concepts.summary: The volume of filtrate formed by both kidneys per minute; about 125 mL a minute in males and 105 mL in females, which is about 180 and 150 litres a day.

concepts.title: Reabsorption
concepts.summary: About 99 percent of the filtrate returns to the circulation, leaving 1 to 2 litres of urine a day.

concepts.title: ADH and aquaporins
concepts.summary: ADH inserts water channels in the collecting ducts; more ADH gives more concentrated urine and less gives dilute urine.

concepts.title: Other kidney jobs
concepts.summary: Regulating pH, helping control blood pressure, making most of the body's erythropoietin and finishing the activation of vitamin D.

concepts.title: Action potential
concepts.summary: A brief electrical signal in which the membrane potential rises from about -70 mV, reaches about +30 mV and returns.

concepts.title: Chemical synapse
concepts.summary: A neurotransmitter released from one cell crosses a small gap and binds to receptors on the next cell.

concepts.title: Sensory receptor and transduction
concepts.summary: Specialised receptor cells change the stimulus into a change in membrane potential.

concepts.title: Reflex arc
concepts.summary: Sensory input, central processing at a synapse in the spinal cord, and motor output, as in withdrawing a hand from a hot stove.

concepts.title: Demyelination
concepts.summary: Loss of the insulation around axons, as in multiple sclerosis, an autoimmune disease affecting the central nervous system.

concepts.title: Hormone and target cell
concepts.summary: A hormone travels in the blood but affects only cells with receptors for it.

concepts.title: Insulin and glucagon
concepts.summary: Insulin, from beta cells, lowers blood glucose; glucagon, from alpha cells, raises it; each is switched off as the level moves back.

concepts.title: Type 2 diabetes
concepts.summary: Cells become resistant to insulin, the pancreas makes more, and over time the beta cells become exhausted.

concepts.title: Early signs of diabetes
concepts.summary: Excessive urination and thirst, because glucose in the filtrate draws water into the urine.

concepts.title: Prevention of type 2 diabetes
concepts.summary: WHO lists a healthy body weight, at least 150 minutes of moderate exercise a week, a healthy diet that avoids sugar and saturated fat, and not smoking.

concepts.title: Innate and adaptive responses
concepts.summary: The innate response is rapid but nonspecific; the adaptive response is slower at a first infection but highly specific and effective.

concepts.title: Antibody and antigen
concepts.summary: An antibody is a protein made by B cells that binds a specific antigen, a structure on the surface of a pathogen.

concepts.title: Immunological memory
concepts.summary: On re-exposure the secondary response is stronger and faster, often clearing the pathogen before any symptoms.

concepts.title: Vaccine
concepts.summary: A killed or weakened pathogen, or its components, that builds immunological memory without causing much in the way of symptoms.

concepts.title: Vaccination coverage
concepts.summary: The share of a group that has received doses; WHO reports it by vaccine and year.

lessons.title: Cells and tissues

lead.text: Early in development the cells that descend from the egg are *undifferentiated*, which means that none of them has yet taken on a particular job. As development continues they **differentiate**: each becomes specialised in its structure and function, so that cells in different places come to look and behave differently.

The differences are large, but they sit on top of a great deal of sameness. The body contains at least 200 distinct cell types, and these cells contain essentially the same internal structures while varying enormously in shape and in what they do, which makes a cell's shape a useful clue to its job.
The cell types are not scattered at random. They occur in organised layers, and a layer of cells that works together on one job is called a **tissue**.

The body's tissues fall into four broad categories. **Epithelial tissue**, also called epithelium, is made of sheets of cells that cover the exterior surfaces of the body, line internal cavities and passageways, and form certain glands. **Connective tissue** binds the cells and organs of the body together and protects, supports and integrates all its parts.

**Muscle tissue** and **nervous tissue** are both *excitable*, which means that they respond to stimulation. Muscle responds by contracting, which provides movement, and it occurs as three major types: skeletal muscle, which is voluntary, smooth muscle, and cardiac muscle in the heart. Nervous tissue responds by propagating electrochemical signals, the nerve impulses that communicate between different regions of the body.

afterFigure.text: Epithelium therefore includes much more than the skin. The same arrangement of tightly packed sheets lines the passageways inside the body, so a sheet of cells on any surface, inside or out, is epithelial, whatever organ it belongs to.

diagram.alt: Four panels of simple drawings. One shows a sheet of tightly packed cells, one shows scattered cells among fibres, one shows long parallel fibres, and one shows a cell with branching extensions. The second view adds each tissue's name and one job.

lead.text: A **stem cell** is an unspecialised cell that can divide without limit as needed and can, under specific conditions, differentiate into specialised cells. The two abilities do different work: dividing keeps up a supply of cells that are still unspecialised, and differentiating turns some of them into the [[specialised cells|Cells that have taken on a particular structure and job. Met in 'Differentiation'.]] that a tissue is made of.

afterFigure.text: Stem cells are divided into several categories according to their potential to differentiate, which is to say according to how many kinds of specialised cell they can give rise to.

diagram.alt: A stem cell on the left. In the first view it divides into two cells that are both still stem cells. In the second it gives rise to three specialised cells with different shapes.
diagram.caption: A stem cell can keep dividing as needed, and under specific conditions it can give rise to specialised cells.

lead.text: Cells do not divide at random. A very elaborate and precise system of regulation directs how a cell proceeds from one phase of the cell cycle to the next and when it begins mitosis, the process in which it divides. The system involves molecules within the cell as well as external triggers, and together these internal and external triggers give the cell "stop" and "advance" signals.
Precise regulation of the cell cycle is critical for maintaining the health of an organism, and **loss of cell cycle control can lead to cancer**.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows the difference in a tissue. While both signals work, division follows them and the layers stay orderly. When the stop signal fails, nothing holds the cells back, and the organisation of the [[tissue|A layer of cells that works together on one job. Met in 'Differentiation'.]] breaks down.

lead.text: A cell escaping its normal control system and becoming cancerous may happen quite frequently throughout the body. Fortunately, certain cells of the immune system can recognise cells that have become cancerous and destroy them. In some cases the cancerous cells remain undetected and continue to proliferate, and the result is a **tumour**.

A tumour that does not pose a threat to surrounding tissues is called **benign**, and it can usually be easily removed. A tumour capable of damage is **malignant**, and the person is diagnosed with cancer. Cancer is therefore a disease of the body's own cells, and it begins when the controls on division fail.
That is an account of how cancer starts, and it stops there. Screening and treatment are not covered here, and they are matters to raise with a doctor or nurse.

lessons.orientation: How one fertilised egg gives rise to many kinds of cell, the four tissues they form, and how cancer starts when the controls on cell division fail.
lessons.nextAction: Explain how the body keeps conditions such as temperature and blood pressure inside a safe range.

blocks.text: You began as a single fertilised egg cell, and the body you see in a mirror is made of trillions of cells that all descend from it. Those cells are far from identical. The body contains at least 200 distinct cell types, which share essentially the same internal structures and yet vary enormously in shape and function.

How one cell becomes so many kinds, how those kinds are arranged into working layers, and what keeps their division in check are the questions behind how organs are built and behind how cancer begins.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to name the four tissue types, match each to its job, and explain cancer as a failure of the controls on cell division.
intro.whyItMatters: Every organ in the lessons that follow is built from these four tissues, and cancer is the standard example of what happens when their organisation breaks down.

recap.keyIdea: One fertilised egg gives rise to many specialised cells, organised into four tissues, and cancer begins when the stop and advance signals that control cell division fail.

blocks.text: Cells **differentiate** as the body develops, and the specialised cells form epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous tissue, each with its own job. A **stem cell** is the unspecialised kind that can divide as needed and give rise to specialised cells.

A cell cycle control system of stop and advance signals decides when cells divide. When it fails, cells can keep dividing, and the tumour that results is benign if it threatens nothing around it and malignant if it can do damage.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks how the body holds values such as temperature and blood pressure steady while the conditions around it change.

lessons.title: Keeping the body steady

lead.text: Every cell has a part in keeping the body's conditions steady, and the name for the result is **homeostasis**: a dynamic state of balance within parameters that are compatible with life. Living cells need a water-based environment, for example, and a number of anatomical and physiological mechanisms keep all of the body's trillions of cells moist, which is one aspect of homeostasis.

The word *dynamic* matters. A value held in homeostasis does not sit at one number, because it moves about inside a range, and core temperature shows this most clearly, with a range of 36.5 to 37.5 degrees Celsius. When a parameter such as blood pressure or blood oxygen content moves far enough out of its range, generally by becoming too high or too low, illness or disease, and sometimes death, inevitably results.

The body regulates its temperature tightly through **thermoregulation**, which keeps core temperature within certain boundaries even when the temperature around it is very different. Part of the heat comes from the cells themselves: in the production of ATP, the molecule cells make to power their work, approximately 60 percent of the energy produced is in the form of heat used to maintain body temperature.

The hypothalamus in the brain does the controlling, and it works as a thermostat. If the temperature is too high, it can start processes that lower it: more blood circulates to the surface of the body, so that heat escapes through the skin, and sweating lets water evaporate from the skin and cool its surface. If the temperature falls below the set core temperature, it can start shivering to generate heat, so that the body uses more energy and makes more heat, and thyroid hormone stimulates more energy use and heat production by cells throughout the body.

afterFigure.text: In both directions the response pushes the temperature back towards the range, which means that the loop acts against whichever change began it. A loop in which the response opposes the change that set it off is called **negative feedback**, and thermoregulation is the textbook's example of it.

lead.text: Negative feedback controls hormones as well as temperature, and there it takes the form of inhibiting further secretion of a hormone once its level is adequate. This allows blood levels of the hormone to be regulated within a narrow range, and the textbook calls it the more common method of hormone regulation.

The release of glucocorticoid hormones from the adrenal glands is an example, directed by the hypothalamus and the pituitary gland. As glucocorticoid concentrations in the blood rise, the hypothalamus and pituitary gland reduce their signalling to the adrenal glands, which prevents additional glucocorticoid secretion, so the hormone switches off its own supply.

The word *negative* names the direction of the response, which opposes the change, and it says nothing about whether the effect is harmful. A negative loop is the ordinary way for the body to hold a value in a narrow range.

reveal.text: The next screen follows the signal from the blood vessels to the heart.

lead.text: Blood pressure is held steady by a loop with the same parts, and here every part has a name. Receptors called **baroreceptors** are stretched by blood pressure. When pressure increases they are stretched more tightly and initiate action potentials, the nerve signals, at a higher rate, and at lower pressures they are stretched less and fire more slowly.

The cardiovascular centre in the medulla oblongata receives this input and triggers a reflex that maintains homeostasis. When pressure rises too high, the baroreceptors fire at a higher rate and the centre triggers parasympathetic stimulation of the heart, as a result of which cardiac output falls, while sympathetic stimulation of the peripheral arterioles decreases and the arterioles widen, a change called vasodilation. Together these changes cause blood pressure to fall.

In the usual language of control loops, the baroreceptors are the *sensors*, the cardiovascular centre is the *control centre*, and the heart and arterioles are the *effectors*, the parts that carry out the correction.

afterFigure.text: The loop also runs the other way. When pressure falls, the baroreceptors are stretched less and fire more slowly, so the control centre receives the opposite report and the same effectors can act in the opposite direction.

lead.text: Some loops add to the change that starts them. In **positive feedback** the release of additional hormone follows an original release, so that the change is amplified. The release of oxytocin during childbirth is the textbook's example: the initial release of oxytocin signals the uterine muscles to contract, which pushes the fetus toward the cervix and stretches it, and the stretch signals the pituitary gland to release more oxytocin, so that labour contractions intensify.

A loop like this has no way of settling at a value, so it runs until something outside it ends it, and here the birth does so, after which the release of oxytocin decreases. Positive feedback is also the less common pattern, since the textbook describes negative feedback as the more common method of hormone regulation.

lessons.orientation: How the body holds values such as temperature and blood pressure within a range by feedback, and how negative feedback differs from positive feedback.
lessons.nextAction: Describe how bone is rebuilt all the time and how muscle contracts, and read the WHO's physical activity figure correctly.

blocks.text: Core body temperature stays at around 36.5 to 37.5 degrees Celsius (97.7 to 99.5 degrees Fahrenheit) even when the temperature around the body is very different. The body achieves this continuously, by detecting a change and acting against it, and it holds blood pressure and blood oxygen content steady in a similar way.

A value that moves far enough out of its range leads to illness, which is why a measurement such as blood pressure is compared with a range and not with a single number. Knowing how the body holds a value steady tells you what a reading of that value is a reading of.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read a value against its range, trace a feedback loop for temperature and for blood pressure, and tell negative feedback from positive feedback.
intro.whyItMatters: A reading such as temperature or blood pressure only means something against the range the body holds it in, and the loops that hold it there are the ones that fail first in illness.

recap.keyIdea: Homeostasis is a dynamic balance within a range, held mostly by negative feedback, which opposes the change that set it off.

blocks.text: Core temperature stays within 36.5 to 37.5 degrees Celsius because the hypothalamus acts as a thermostat, and blood pressure stays in range because baroreceptors report to the cardiovascular centre, which adjusts the heart and arterioles. Both loops are **negative feedback**, in which the response opposes the change that began it.
**Positive feedback** adds to the change instead, as the oxytocin loop of labour does, and it runs only until something outside the loop, here the birth, ends it.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at bones and muscles, which are living tissues that the body keeps rebuilding and that respond to how much they are used.

lessons.title: Bones and muscles

lead.text: Bone is dynamic: new tissue is constantly formed, and old, injured or unnecessary bone is dissolved for repair or for the release of calcium. Two kinds of cell do this work. The cell responsible for bone breakdown, which is called **resorption**, is the **osteoclast**, and osteoclasts are found on bone surfaces and are multinucleated, meaning that each has many nuclei.

Osteoclasts are continually breaking down old bone while **osteoblasts** are continually forming new bone. The ongoing balance between the two is responsible for the constant but subtle reshaping of bone.

Because bone is rebuilt all the time, the balance between breakdown and formation decides whether bone mass is kept, gained or lost. **Osteoporosis** is a disease characterised by a decrease in bone mass that occurs when the rate of bone resorption exceeds the rate of bone formation, and it is a common occurrence as the body ages.

afterFigure.text: The textbook contrasts this with Paget's disease, in which overactive osteoclasts break bone down and new bone is formed in an attempt to keep up, but the new bone is produced haphazardly. A physician evaluating thinning bone therefore tests for both diseases, as well as others.

Use also affects the balance. The textbook summarises controlled studies in which people who exercise regularly have greater bone density than those who are more sedentary. Any type of exercise stimulates the deposition of more bone tissue, but resistance training has a greater effect than cardiovascular activities, and it is especially important for slowing the eventual loss of bone with ageing and for preventing osteoporosis.

lead.text: A muscle begins to contract, which means to shorten, when a protein called **actin** is pulled by a protein called **myosin**. In striated muscle, meaning skeletal and cardiac muscle, this happens after specific binding sites on the actin have been exposed by the interaction of calcium ions with two proteins that shield those sites. Smooth muscle uses calcium in a different way and is left out here.

All muscles require [[ATP|The molecule cells make to power their work. Met in 'Keeping the body steady'.]] to continue the process of contracting, and they relax when the calcium is removed and the binding sites are shielded again.

afterFigure.text: What the figure shows is a **sarcomere**, the repeating unit in which actin and myosin overlap. Each muscle fibre, which is a single long muscle cell, holds many sarcomeres in chains called myofibrils.

reveal.text: The next screen gives the textbook's account of what use and disuse do to a muscle.

lead.text: The number of skeletal muscle fibres in a given muscle is genetically determined and does not change. Muscle strength is directly related to the amount of myofibrils and sarcomeres within each fibre, so a muscle changes by adding or losing contracting machinery inside fibres that stay the same in number.

Factors such as hormones and stress acting on the muscle can increase the production of sarcomeres and myofibrils, a change called **hypertrophy**, which results in increased mass and bulk. Decreased use has the opposite effect. In **atrophy** the sarcomeres and myofibrils disappear, but the number of muscle fibres does not, and it is common for a limb in a cast to show atrophied muscles when the cast is removed.

The World Health Organization states that physical inactivity is one of the leading risk factors for deaths from noncommunicable diseases, and that people who are insufficiently active have a 20 to 30 percent increased risk of death compared with people who are sufficiently active. It adds that in adults, regular physical activity is *associated* with a lower risk of death from all causes and from cardiovascular disease, with fewer new cases of high blood pressure and of type 2 diabetes, and with fewer falls.

A figure like this compares two groups, and **a percentage increase in risk is taken of the risk that the comparison group already has**. It is called a **relative risk** for that reason, and it is not the same thing as a number of extra deaths per hundred, because the same percentage gives a different count when the starting risk is different.

The figure describes groups and says what is associated with what. It does not predict what will happen to any one person, and it is not advice to any one person about how much activity to do, which is a question for a doctor or nurse.

steps.headline: Invented figures: 40 in 1,000 sufficiently active adults die in a study period. Find the range for a comparable group with a 20 to 30 percent higher risk.

workedSteps.text: A 20 percent increase is 20 percent of the baseline of 40 deaths per 1,000.
Adding the extra deaths to the baseline gives the lower end of the range.
A 30 percent increase is 30 percent of the same baseline.
Adding these extra deaths to the baseline gives the upper end of the range.
The insufficiently active group would have 48 to 52 deaths per 1,000, which is 8 to 12 more than the baseline and not 20 to 30 more.

steps.headline: Invented figures: 60 in 1,000 sufficiently active adults die during a study period. Find the range for a comparable insufficiently active group.

workedSteps.text: A 20 percent increase is 20 percent of the baseline of 60.
Add that increase to the baseline to find the lower end of the range.
A 30 percent increase is 30 percent of the same baseline.
Add that increase to the baseline to find the upper end of the range.

lessons.orientation: How bone is constantly rebuilt, how muscle contracts and changes with use and disuse, and how to read the WHO's relative risk for physical inactivity.
lessons.nextAction: Follow blood through the heart's four chambers and two circuits, and calculate cardiac output.

blocks.text: Bone seems the least changeable part of the body, yet the textbook calls it dynamic: new bone tissue is constantly formed, and old, injured or unnecessary bone is dissolved for repair or for the release of calcium. Muscle changes as well, growing with use and wasting with disuse.

Both tissues respond to how much they are used, and that response is part of why physical activity appears in public health figures. Reading one of those figures correctly, the World Health Organization's statement of how much higher the risk of death is for people who are insufficiently active, takes a piece of arithmetic that is easy to get wrong.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to name the cells that build and break down bone, explain how muscle changes with use and disuse, and apply a relative risk to a baseline.
intro.whyItMatters: Bone and muscle both respond to use, and a relative risk is the form in which the WHO states its figure for physical inactivity and the risk of death.

recap.keyIdea: Bone is rebuilt all the time by osteoblasts and osteoclasts, muscle shortens when myosin pulls actin, and a relative risk is a percentage of the baseline and not a count.

blocks.text: **Osteoblasts** form bone and **osteoclasts** break it down, and when resorption runs ahead of formation bone mass falls, as in osteoporosis. Muscle contracts when calcium exposes binding sites on actin and myosin pulls, using ATP, and use and disuse change the amount of sarcomeres and myofibrils in each fibre without changing the number of fibres.
The WHO's 20 to 30 percent increased risk is a **relative risk**, taken of the baseline, so a baseline of 50 in 1,000 gives 60 to 65 and not 70 to 80.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to the heart, which is cardiac muscle, and calculates how much blood it pumps each minute.

lessons.title: The heart

lead.text: The human heart has four chambers: the left side and the right side each have one **atrium** and one **ventricle**. Each of the upper chambers, the right atrium and the left atrium, acts as a receiving chamber and contracts to push blood into the lower chambers, the right ventricle and the left ventricle. The ventricles are the primary pumping chambers of the heart, and they propel blood to the lungs or to the rest of the body.

The wall of the heart is [[cardiac muscle|Muscle tissue of the heart, one of the three major types of muscle. Met in 'Cells and tissues'.]], so each chamber pumps by contracting, in the way described in the last lesson.

Blood travels through two distinct but linked circuits, the **pulmonary circuit** and the **systemic circuit**, and the simplest way to tell them apart is by the gases they carry. The pulmonary circuit takes blood to and from the lungs, where it picks up oxygen and delivers carbon dioxide for exhalation. The systemic circuit takes oxygenated blood to virtually all of the tissues of the body and returns relatively deoxygenated blood, with carbon dioxide, to the heart, to be sent back into the pulmonary circuit.

The blood leaving the systemic capillaries is lower in oxygen than when it entered. The capillaries unite into venules and then into ever larger veins, which flow into the two major systemic veins, the superior vena cava and the inferior vena cava. These return blood to the right atrium, which pumps it into the right ventricle, and the process continues for as long as the person is alive.

afterFigure.text: The two circuits are joined end to end, which makes the two sides of the heart pumps in series: blood leaves the right ventricle for the lungs, returns to the left atrium, and only then is pumped to the body by the left ventricle.

lead.text: **Cardiac output** is a measurement of the amount of blood pumped by each ventricle in one minute. To calculate it, multiply the **stroke volume**, the amount of blood pumped by each ventricle in one beat, by the heart rate, in beats per minute.

When stroke volume is in millilitres and heart rate is in beats per minute, the product comes out in millilitres per minute. Dividing by 1,000 converts it to litres per minute, because a litre is 1,000 millilitres.

steps.headline: A resting adult's ventricle pumps 70 mL a beat at 75 beats per minute. Find the cardiac output in litres per minute.

workedSteps.text: Cardiac output is stroke volume multiplied by heart rate.
Putting in the values gives the output in millilitres per minute.
A litre is 1,000 millilitres, so the last step divides by 1,000.
The cardiac output is 5.25 litres per minute.

lead.text: In healthy young people the heart rate may increase to 150 beats per minute during exercise. The stroke volume can also increase, from 70 to approximately 130 mL, because each contraction becomes stronger. Both factors in the product rise together, and the cardiac output increases to approximately 19.5 litres per minute. Top cardiovascular athletes can achieve even higher levels.

afterFigure.text: Neither factor accounts for the whole increase on its own. A heart rate of 150 beats per minute with the resting stroke volume of 70 mL would give 10,500 mL, or 10.5 litres, per minute, and the rest of the rise comes from the stronger beat.

steps.headline: During exercise a healthy young adult's heart rate is 150 beats per minute and the stroke volume is 130 mL. Find the cardiac output in litres per minute.

workedSteps.text: Cardiac output is stroke volume multiplied by heart rate.
Multiply the two values to get the output in millilitres per minute.
Divide by 1,000 to convert the output to litres per minute.

lead.text: For an adult, a normal resting heart rate is in the range of 60 to 100 beats per minute. A resting rate below 60 is called **bradycardia**, and a resting rate above 100 is called **tachycardia**. Trained athletes typically have very low heart rates.

The textbook adds that when a person has no other symptoms, such as weakness, fatigue, dizziness, fainting, chest discomfort, palpitations or respiratory distress, bradycardia is not considered clinically significant. If any of those symptoms are present, they may indicate that the heart is not providing sufficient oxygenated blood to the tissues. The number is therefore only part of the picture, and what a particular number means for a particular person is a question for a doctor or nurse.

The World Health Organization monitors trends in physical inactivity. A recent study it cites found that nearly one third of the world's adults, 31 percent or 1.8 billion people, do not meet the global recommendation of at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity per week. That is an increase of five percentage points between 2010 and 2022, and if the trend continues the share is projected to reach 35 percent by 2030.

The wording matters. Five *percentage points* is the difference between two percentages of the same group, which is a different quantity from the five percent that a [[relative increase|A percentage taken of a baseline, so it is not a count. Met in 'Bones and muscles'.]] would mean. Exercise is also the situation in which the heart's rate and stroke volume rise, as the earlier figure showed.
The question is about how the textbook reads a number and is not a judgement about anyone's own heart.

lessons.orientation: How blood moves through the heart's four chambers and two circuits, how cardiac output is calculated from stroke volume and heart rate, and how a resting heart rate is read.
lessons.nextAction: Put the vessels in order along the path of blood, and read a blood pressure as systolic over diastolic.

blocks.text: In healthy young people the heart rate may rise to 150 beats per minute during exercise while each beat sends out more blood, and together the two changes raise the amount of blood pumped each minute to approximately 19.5 litres. That amount is the product of two numbers that can be measured, and one of them, the heart rate, is among the most familiar numbers in health information.
The heart that produces them is a pump with four chambers feeding two circuits, and knowing how it is built shows what the numbers describe and how they can be calculated.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to follow blood through the heart's chambers and circuits, calculate cardiac output from stroke volume and heart rate, and read a resting heart rate against the normal range.
intro.whyItMatters: Heart rate and the amount of blood the heart moves each minute are numbers you can calculate and read against a range, and the same few steps work for any values.

recap.keyIdea: Blood runs through two circuits joined end to end by a four-chambered pump, and cardiac output is stroke volume multiplied by heart rate.

blocks.text: Blood passes from the right atrium to the right ventricle, through the lungs, to the left atrium, to the left ventricle and around the body, and **cardiac output** is the stroke volume multiplied by the heart rate. Exercise raises both factors, which takes the output from about 5.25 litres per minute at rest to about 19.5 in the textbook's examples.
A normal adult resting rate is 60 to 100 beats per minute, with **bradycardia** below and **tachycardia** above, and trained athletes typically have very low rates.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson follows blood once it leaves the heart, through the vessels, and asks what a blood pressure reading measures.

lessons.title: Blood vessels and blood pressure

lead.text: Blood is a **connective tissue**, which means that, like bone or cartilage, it consists of cells set in a surrounding material. The cells are known as the formed elements, and there are three kinds of them: red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets, which are fragments of cells. The material around them is called **plasma**, and it makes blood unusual among connective tissues because it is a fluid, mostly water, which keeps the formed elements suspended and lets them circulate through the cardiovascular system.
The tubes that carry this fluid, and the pressure it exerts inside them, come next.

Blood travels through the body in blood vessels. It leaves the heart in an **artery**, a vessel that carries blood *away* from the heart, and the artery branches into ever smaller vessels. The smallest arteries are the **arterioles**, and they branch in turn into the **capillaries**, tiny vessels in which nutrients and wastes are exchanged. Beyond the capillaries the vessels join together again, first as **venules**, small vessels that lead to a vein, and then as a **vein**, a larger vessel that returns blood to the heart.

afterFigure.text: The names follow direction and not contents: an artery is any vessel carrying blood away from the heart, and a vein is any vessel carrying it back. The exchange between blood and tissue happens in the capillaries, so the other vessels in the loop serve as the road to that exchange and the road home from it.

diagram.alt: A loop of boxes. The heart leads to an artery, then an arteriole, then a capillary, then a venule, then a vein, and the vein leads back to the heart. Three views highlight the stretch away from the heart, the exchange in the capillary, and the return.

lead.text: Pressure in the arteries is not constant, because the heart delivers blood in pulses. Each time the ventricles, the lower chambers of the heart, contract, they eject blood into the arteries and the pressure there climbs to its highest value. Between beats the ventricles relax and the pressure falls to its lowest, and the figure shows both movements over three heartbeats.

afterFigure.text: A blood pressure is therefore recorded as a ratio of two numbers, the **systolic pressure** over the **diastolic pressure**. The systolic pressure is the higher value, typically around 120 mm Hg, and it reflects the ejection of blood during the ventricles' contraction, which is called systole. The diastolic pressure is the lower value, usually about 80 mm Hg, and it is the pressure during relaxation, or diastole. The unit mm Hg is millimetres of mercury, and OpenStax gives 120/80 as an example of a normal adult blood pressure. Put another way, the first number is the pressure when the heart beats and the second is the pressure when it rests between beats.

diagram.alt: A graph of arterial pressure over three heartbeats. The pressure rises quickly to a peak of about 120 mm Hg and falls slowly to about 80 mm Hg before the next beat. Later views mark the peak and the lowest point and write them as 120/80.
diagram.caption: Pressure in an artery over three heartbeats. Use the buttons to mark the peak and the lowest point and to write them as a reading.

steps.headline: A reading is 118/76. Say what each number is.

workedSteps.text: The first number is the larger one, and it is always the systolic pressure.
The second number is the smaller one, and it is the diastolic pressure.

The systolic pressure is the pressure while the ventricles contract, and the diastolic is the pressure while they relax, so the pressure in the arteries swings between the two numbers with each heartbeat.

steps.headline: A reading is 120/80. Find how far the systolic pressure is above the diastolic pressure.

workedSteps.text: The first number is the systolic pressure.
The second number is the diastolic pressure.
The gap between the two is found by taking the smaller from the larger. Work it out.

lead.text: Think about what a person with raised blood pressure would be aware of.

reveal.text: The World Health Organization says that people with high blood pressure may not feel symptoms, and that the only way to know is to get the pressure checked. The next screen turns that into numbers.

lead.text: Because symptoms cannot be relied on, high blood pressure is defined by numbers, and the numbers depend on where the reading is taken. The NHS says that a person is usually considered to have high blood pressure when a reading checked by a healthcare professional is 140/90 or higher, or when a reading checked at home is 135/85 or higher. The WHO describes **hypertension**, the medical name for high blood pressure, as a pressure of 140/90 mm Hg or higher.

afterFigure.text: The home figure is lower than the clinic figure, so the same reading can lie above the line in one setting and below it in the other. A reading is never only a pair of numbers: it is a pair with a setting attached. The lines in this lesson are the two organisations' own, and a different guideline may place its line elsewhere. The examples here also keep both numbers on the same side of a line, because the pages quoted do not settle a case in which only one of them reaches it.

lead.text: A single high reading is a reason to measure again and not a diagnosis. The WHO diagnoses hypertension when readings taken on two different days show a systolic pressure of 140 or higher on both days, a diastolic pressure of 90 or higher on both days, or both. The NHS describes confirming a high clinic reading with further checks, such as readings taken at home or monitoring over 24 hours.

This lesson explains what the numbers mean, and it cannot say what any one person's reading means. Anyone with a concern about their own blood pressure should have a health professional take the reading.

The WHO divides the risk factors for high blood pressure into those that can be changed and those that cannot. The **modifiable** ones include a diet high in salt and in saturated and trans fats, a low intake of fruit and vegetables, physical inactivity, tobacco, alcohol, and being overweight or obese, and the WHO adds air pollution as the most significant environmental factor. The **non-modifiable** ones are a family history of hypertension, an age over 65, and co-existing diseases such as diabetes or kidney disease.
Salt, the first item on that list, is a subject the nutrition lesson returns to. A factor being modifiable describes the factor, and it says nothing about what any one person ought to do.
A man leaves a clinic with a reading in his hand.

reveal.text: The NHS and the WHO both treat a single reading above the line as a prompt for more readings. The reading starts the process of finding out and does not finish it.

lessons.orientation: Put the blood vessels in order, read a blood pressure as systolic over diastolic, and see why one reading is not a diagnosis.
lessons.nextAction: Say how pressure differences move air in and out of the lungs and how oxygen crosses into the blood.

blocks.text: A blood pressure reading is written as two numbers, such as 120/80, and the first of them is always the larger. Each number measures the pressure of the blood in the vessels at a different moment of the heartbeat, so the pair describes a pressure that rises and falls with every beat and does not stay constant.

Reading the pair correctly matters because high blood pressure usually gives no warning. The World Health Organization says that people with it may not feel symptoms and that the only way to know is to have the pressure checked, which makes the numbers, and what they do and do not show, worth understanding.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to put the blood vessels in order, read a blood pressure as systolic over diastolic, and say why one high reading is not a diagnosis.
intro.whyItMatters: High blood pressure rarely announces itself, so reading the numbers correctly is often the only way a problem is found.

recap.keyIdea: Blood passes from arteries through capillaries to veins, and its pressure is written as systolic over diastolic and judged against lines that depend on the setting and on more than one reading.

blocks.text: Blood leaves the heart in arteries, which branch to arterioles and then to capillaries, where the exchange takes place, and returns through venules and veins. Its pressure rises to the systolic value as the ventricles contract and falls to the diastolic value as they relax. The NHS and the WHO set their lines at 140/90 for a clinic and 135/85 at home, and the WHO asks for readings on two different days, so one reading starts a check and does not complete it.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson follows the blood into the lungs, where it picks up oxygen and gives up carbon dioxide.

lessons.title: Lungs and breathing

lead.text: When you breathe, your lungs take in oxygen from the air and deliver it to the bloodstream, because the cells of the body need oxygen to work and grow. Carbon dioxide travels the other way, from the blood into the air in the lungs, and is breathed out. The exchange happens in the **alveoli**, the many tiny air spaces of the lungs, which lie against the capillaries that carry blood through them.
Everything else about breathing, from the muscles that move the chest to the count of breaths in a minute, serves to keep fresh air on one side of that exchange and blood moving on the other.

The wall of an alveolus is a single layer of flat cells attached to a thin, elastic basement membrane, and it lies directly against the wall of a capillary. Taken together, the alveolar wall and the capillary wall form the **respiratory membrane**, which is approximately 0.5 micrometres thick. A micrometre is a thousandth of a millimetre, so one millimetre contains 1,000 micrometres, and the membrane is a very small fraction of a millimetre across.

Gases cross this membrane by **simple diffusion**, which means that particles drift from where there are more of them to where there are fewer, without the cells spending energy on the movement. Oxygen is picked up by the blood for transport, and carbon dioxide is released into the air of the alveoli.

reveal.text: The diaphragm and the intercostal muscles, which lie between the ribs, make most of the pressure changes of breathing, and the lungs themselves are passive. The next screen follows the steps.

lead.text: Breathing depends on pressure differences. Air moves from a region of higher pressure to a region of lower pressure, so for air to enter the lungs the pressure inside them, which the textbook calls the **intrapulmonary pressure**, has to fall below the pressure of the air outside, the atmospheric pressure. The lungs do not bring this about themselves, because they are passive. The work is done by the diaphragm, the sheet of muscle beneath the lungs, and by the intercostal muscles between the ribs.

afterFigure.text: When these muscles contract, the chest cavity enlarges. A thin film of pleural fluid holds the lungs against the inside of the chest wall, so when the wall moves outward the lungs are pulled outward with it and their volume rises. The same amount of air now fills a larger space, the intrapulmonary pressure falls below atmospheric pressure, and air flows in through the airways.

In the breath in view the chest is larger, the diaphragm is flatter, air moves in and a gauge shows pressure below atmospheric. In the breath out view the chest is smaller, the diaphragm is domed, air moves out and the gauge shows pressure above atmospheric.

lead.text: Breathing out normally takes no muscular effort, which surprises many people. This **passive expiration** works because lung tissue is elastic. When the diaphragm and the intercostal muscles relax after a breath in, the elasticity of the lung tissue makes the lungs recoil, and the chest cavity and the lungs decrease in volume.

afterFigure.text: The air is now squeezed into a smaller space, so the intrapulmonary pressure rises above atmospheric pressure, and the pressure difference pushes air out of the lungs. The sequence is the breath in run backwards, with one difference: in a breath in the muscles start working, and in a breath out they stop.

lead.text: Breathing usually happens without thought, although you can take control of it, for example when you swim under water, sing or blow bubbles. The **respiratory rate** is the number of breaths, or respiratory cycles, in each minute. It is set by the respiratory centre, a region of the brain in the medulla oblongata, which responds primarily to changes in the levels of carbon dioxide, oxygen and pH in the blood, so that low oxygen is one signal among several.

afterFigure.text: A normal rate changes with age. A child under 1 year old breathes between 30 and 60 times a minute, a child of about 10 years closer to 18 to 30, and by adolescence the rate is similar to an adult's, 12 to 18 breaths a minute. Rate matters in health because it can be an important indicator of disease, since it may rise or fall during an illness, although a count on its own does not say what lies behind it. These are the ranges the textbook gives, and other references may draw them a little differently.

steps.headline: MedlinePlus says you breathe nearly 25,000 times in a normal day. Find about how many breaths that is each minute.

workedSteps.text: A day has 24 hours, and each hour has 60 minutes.
Share the breaths in a day among the minutes in a day.
Work out the division and round it to the nearest whole number.

lead.text: Tobacco smoke and second-hand smoke are both considered carcinogenic, which means that they can cause cancer, and exposure to second-hand smoke can cause lung cancer in people who do not use tobacco themselves. OpenStax reports an estimate that the risk of lung cancer is increased by *up to* 30 percent in nonsmokers who live with a person who smokes in the house, compared with nonsmokers who are not regularly exposed. Children are especially affected: those who live with someone who smokes indoors have more lower respiratory infections, which are associated with hospitalisations, more ear infections, and worse symptoms of asthma.

A figure of this kind is a **relative increase**, a percentage of the risk that was already there and not a number of extra cases by itself. Suppose, with an invented baseline, that 20 in every 1,000 unexposed nonsmokers develop a disease. An increase of 30 percent is 30 percent of 20, which is 6, so the exposed group would have 26 in every 1,000. The words "up to" matter too, because they mean that the increase may be smaller than 30 percent.

reveal.text: The invented numbers show how to apply a relative increase. They say nothing about how common lung cancer actually is.

lessons.orientation: Explain how pressure differences move air in and out, how gases cross the respiratory membrane, and how a respiratory rate is read against its ranges.
lessons.nextAction: Follow food along the alimentary canal and say what the small intestine does that the stomach does not.

blocks.text: Air does not flow into your lungs because the lungs draw it in. It flows because the pressure inside the chest falls below the pressure of the air outside, and the lungs themselves take no active part in making that happen. The muscles around them do the work, and a breath out, remarkably, needs no work at all.

All of this serves an exchange across a wall about 0.5 micrometres thick, where oxygen passes from the air into the blood and carbon dioxide passes the other way. Understanding how the pressure is made, and how many breaths a minute are usual at different ages, is what makes sense of both the exchange and the way a breathing rate is read.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to order the steps of a breath, convert a thickness from micrometres to millimetres, and read a breathing rate against the ranges for each age.
intro.whyItMatters: A breathing rate is among the simplest measurements in health, and reading a risk such as second-hand smoke correctly depends on the same habit of working with numbers.

recap.keyIdea: Air moves because the diaphragm and rib muscles change the pressure in the lungs, gases cross a membrane about 0.5 micrometres thick, and a breathing rate is read against the range for the person's age.

blocks.text: The diaphragm and intercostal muscles enlarge the chest, which lowers the pressure in the lungs below atmospheric pressure and draws air in, while a normal breath out is passive because the elastic lungs recoil. Oxygen and carbon dioxide cross the respiratory membrane by simple diffusion, and the respiratory rate of 12 to 18 breaths a minute for adolescents and adults is an indicator that rises or falls in illness. A figure such as an increase of up to 30 percent is a share of an existing risk, so it is applied to a baseline.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson follows food along the alimentary canal, where a different kind of exchange takes nutrients into the blood.

lessons.title: Digestion

lead.text: The alimentary canal, also called the gastrointestinal tract or the gut, is a one-way tube that begins at the mouth and ends at the anus. Between those two points it is modified into the pharynx, the esophagus, the stomach, and the small and large intestines, each fitted to a different part of the work of nourishing the body. Because both ends open to the external environment, food and wastes inside the canal are technically considered to be outside the body, and only **absorption**, the passage of nutrients across the lining, brings them into the body's inner space.

afterFigure.text: The figure sets out the organs in the order food meets them. In life the canal is about 7.62 metres long, and it measures closer to 10.67 metres after death, once the tone of its smooth muscle is lost.

diagram.alt: The six parts of the alimentary canal stacked in the order food meets them: mouth, pharynx, esophagus, stomach, small intestine and large intestine, joined by arrows. A second view gives each part's job in a line.

lead.text: Food leaves the mouth when the tongue and the pharyngeal muscles propel it into the esophagus. This act of swallowing is the last voluntary act until defecation, and it is an example of **propulsion**, the movement of food through the digestive tract. From then on the movement is involuntary and is carried out by **peristalsis**, sequential, alternating waves of contraction and relaxation of the smooth muscle in the wall of the canal. The same waves help to mix food with digestive juices, and they are so powerful that food and liquid you swallow reach your stomach even if you are standing on your head.

reveal.text: The textbook calls the stomach a temporary holding chamber. The next screen follows what happens to the food while it waits.

lead.text: Popular culture tends to describe the stomach as the place where all digestion happens, and the textbook is direct about this: it is not true. An important function of the stomach is to serve as a temporary holding chamber, because a meal can be eaten far more quickly than the small intestine can digest and absorb it. The stomach therefore holds the food and lets small amounts pass into the small intestine at a time, a **controlled release**. While the food waits it is mixed with digestive juices until it has been converted into **chyme**, and it is not processed in the order in which it was eaten, because the whole meal is mixed together.

Food that has been broken down is of no value to the body unless its nutrients enter the bloodstream, and this happens through absorption, which takes place primarily in the small intestine. There most nutrients cross the epithelial cells that line the canal and enter the bloodstream. Lipids take a different route: they are absorbed into vessels called lacteals and are carried by the lymphatic vessels to the bloodstream, which they reach near the heart.

afterFigure.text: Three features of the lining, the **circular folds**, the **villi** and the **microvilli**, together increase the absorptive surface of the small intestine more than 600-fold. Each is a fold, finger or bump on a smaller scale than the one before it, so that a tube of modest length carries a very large area of lining. These adaptations are most abundant in the first two thirds of the small intestine, where the majority of absorption occurs.

diagram.alt: Three views of the lining of the small intestine, each zoomed in on the one before. The first shows large circular folds, the second shows finger-shaped villi covering a fold, and the third shows the tiny microvilli on the edge of one cell of a villus.

lead.text: Lactose intolerance is a condition characterised by indigestion caused by dairy products. It occurs when the absorptive cells of the small intestine do not produce enough **lactase**, the **enzyme** that digests the milk sugar lactose. An enzyme is a protein that speeds up a chemical reaction, and different digestive enzymes work on different ingredients, so a shortage of one leaves its own ingredient undigested while everything else in the meal is handled as usual.

The condition is common among mammals, since in most of them lactose intolerance increases with age, whereas some human populations keep the ability to produce lactase as adults. It shows in a single case that digestion is more than moving food along the canal: the chemical breakdown has to happen as well, and each step depends on its own enzyme.

reveal.text: A shortage of one enzyme affects only the food that enzyme digests, which is why the indigestion in this case follows dairy products and not every meal.

lessons.orientation: Follow food along the alimentary canal, tell the digestive processes apart, and see what lactose intolerance shows about enzymes.
lessons.nextAction: Trace how carbohydrate becomes ATP, split a day's energy, and apply the WHO's limits for sugar and salt.

blocks.text: The alimentary canal, the tube that runs from the mouth to the anus, is about 7.62 metres long in life, and the food inside it is strictly still outside the body. Both ends of the tube are open to the external environment, so a mouthful that has been swallowed has not yet entered the body's inner space, and it does so only when its nutrients are absorbed through the lining.

That one fact organises the whole of digestion. The parts of the canal exist to push food along, to mix it with juices, to break it down and to absorb what it holds, and each of these is a separate job done by a different part. Following a mouthful from end to end also shows what happens when one small step fails, as it does in lactose intolerance.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to put the parts of the canal in order, tell propulsion, mixing and absorption apart, and explain what a shortage of lactase does.
intro.whyItMatters: Knowing which part of the canal does which job explains why a problem with one enzyme shows up after one kind of food.

recap.keyIdea: Food travels one way along the alimentary canal, and different parts push it, mix it, release it and absorb it, with most absorption in the small intestine.

blocks.text: A mouthful passes from the mouth through the pharynx and esophagus to the stomach and then the small and large intestines, and it counts as inside the body only once its nutrients are absorbed. Peristalsis propels it, the stomach mixes it into chyme and releases it in small amounts, and the folds, villi and microvilli of the small intestine enlarge the surface for absorption more than 600-fold. Lactose intolerance shows that digestion also needs enzymes, because too little lactase leaves the milk sugar undigested.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson follows the nutrients once they are absorbed, from glucose to ATP, and looks at how much energy the body uses.

lessons.title: Nutrition and energy

lead.text: Glucose is the body's most readily available source of energy. Once digestion has broken polysaccharides down into monosaccharides, including glucose, the sugars are transported across the wall of the small intestine into the circulatory system, which carries them to the liver. In the liver, cells either pass the glucose on through the circulation or store the excess as glycogen. Cells around the body then take up the circulating glucose in response to insulin, and through a series of reactions called glycolysis they transfer some of its energy to form **ATP**, the molecule that cells use to hold energy ready for work.

afterFigure.text: The route has two stretches, shown in the figure: glucose travels from the gut to the liver and the circulation, and then it is taken up by cells and processed by glycolysis. The textbook says that glycolysis transfers *some* of the energy in glucose to ATP, so the energy in the sugar is not all passed on at that step.

diagram.alt: A row of five boxes: carbohydrate, glucose, liver, body cells and ATP, joined by arrows. One view highlights the stretch from the gut to the liver, and the other the stretch inside cells.
diagram.caption: The route from carbohydrate in food to ATP in cells, in two stretches. Use the buttons to move between them.

lead.text: The energy a person needs or takes in each day is measured in calories, and the unit used for food is the nutritional **Calorie**, the amount of heat needed to raise 1 kg (1,000 g) of water by 1 °C. The calorie of the physical sciences is smaller: it is the heat needed to raise only 1 g of water by 1 °C. A nutritional Calorie is therefore 1,000 times as large, since 1 kg holds 1,000 g.
A capital C marks the nutritional unit throughout this lesson. Food labels and the WHO page, which writes "calories", use the same word for the same unit.

reveal.text: The textbook puts the largest share of a day's energy into the basic functions of the organs. The next screen gives all three shares.

lead.text: The body uses energy even at rest. The **basal metabolic rate**, or BMR, is the amount of daily energy that a person uses at rest, in a neutrally warm environment, and it measures how much energy the body needs for normal, basic, daily activity. About 70 percent of all daily energy expenditure comes from the basic functions of the organs, another 20 percent from physical activity, and the remaining 10 percent from keeping the body temperature steady.

afterFigure.text: These are the textbook's percentages for energy used in a day, so the amounts scale with the total, as the figure shows for two invented totals. The rate is higher in someone who is more active or has more lean body mass, and it generally decreases with age as the proportion of muscle falls.

steps.headline: A person uses 2,500 Calories in a day. Split that energy into its three uses.

workedSteps.text: Basic functions of the organs take 70 percent of the total.
Physical activity takes 20 percent.
Temperature control takes the remaining 10 percent.
The three parts should add up to the whole day, which checks the working.

lead.text: The WHO describes a healthy diet through four principles that apply together. **Adequacy** means meeting needs for nutrients without exceeding them, so that deficiencies are prevented. **Balance** means that the energy taken in matches the energy used, with a suitable balance among the three main sources of energy, protein, fats and carbohydrates. **Moderation** means limiting nutrients, ingredients and foods that may be detrimental to health, and **diversity** means including a wide variety of nutritious foods within and across food groups.

afterFigure.text: These are principles and not a menu. The WHO says that the detail of a healthy diet varies with a person's age, culture and the food available, so the principles stay the same while the foods differ.

diagram.alt: A table of the four WHO principles of a healthy diet. Adequacy meets needs without exceeding them, balance matches energy in to energy out, moderation limits foods that may harm health, and diversity asks for a wide variety of nutritious foods.
diagram.caption: The four principles apply together, and none of them replaces the others.

cases.label: The four principles

lead.text: Moderation is where the WHO gives numbers. It says that free sugars should make up less than 10 percent of total daily energy intake, which it equates to 50 g, or about 12 level teaspoons, for a person of healthy body weight who eats about 2,000 Calories a day, and it adds that 5 percent or less may bring further health benefits. For salt, it says that adults should take in less than 5 grams a day, which is 2 grams of sodium. These are limits for adults in general, and they are not a prescription for any one person.

afterFigure.text: Salt belongs in this lesson because of the link back to [[blood pressure|The pressure of the blood in the vessels, written as systolic over diastolic. Met in 'Blood vessels and blood pressure'.]]: the WHO says that high sodium intake is associated with increased blood pressure, which can lead to cardiovascular disease, and that people are often unaware of how much salt they take in. It adds that potassium can mitigate the effect of high sodium on blood pressure.

reveal.text: The limit is a total for the day from every source, so a single dish that uses up most of it leaves little for anything else.

lessons.orientation: Trace how carbohydrate becomes ATP, split a day's energy into its three uses, and work with the WHO's principles and its limits for sugar and salt.
lessons.nextAction: Follow how the kidneys filter the blood and keep the body's water in balance.

blocks.text: Glucose is the body's most readily available source of energy, and its route from a mouthful of bread to the energy a cell holds ready for use passes through most of what has been covered so far: the gut, the blood and the liver. The same chain explains why food energy is counted in a unit that is larger than the one physicists use.

Where that energy goes once it is in the cells, and what the World Health Organization says about sugar and salt, can be worked out with a few percentages. The WHO figures describe populations and typical adults, so here they are numbers to work with and not advice about what anyone should eat.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to order the route from carbohydrate to ATP, split a day's energy by the textbook's percentages, and apply a WHO limit to a number.
intro.whyItMatters: Food labels and health guidance use percentages and grams, and reading them correctly is the same skill as the arithmetic of this lesson.

recap.keyIdea: Carbohydrate becomes glucose and then ATP, about 70, 20 and 10 percent of a day's energy go to the organs, activity and temperature, and the WHO states its limits for sugar and salt as percentages and grams.

blocks.text: Digested carbohydrate crosses the wall of the small intestine as glucose, passes through the liver, and is taken up by cells in response to insulin, where glycolysis transfers some of its energy to ATP. A day's energy use divides into about 70 percent for the organs, 20 percent for activity and 10 percent for temperature, measured in nutritional Calories, which are 1,000 times the physicist's calorie. The WHO's four principles are adequacy, balance, moderation and diversity, and its limits of under 10 percent of energy from free sugars and under 5 grams of salt are figures for adults in general.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to the kidneys, which keep the amount of water and dissolved substances in the body steady.

lessons.title: Kidneys and water balance

lead.text: You have two kidneys, each about the size of your fist, near the middle of your back just below the rib cage. Inside each one are about a million tiny structures called **nephrons**, and every nephron filters blood, taking out wastes and extra water. Those wastes and that water become urine (MedlinePlus, National Library of Medicine).

The urine does not leave straight away. It flows from each kidney through a tube called a **ureter** into the **bladder**, which stores it until you go to the bathroom, and the figure follows that path from the kidneys to the outside.

diagram.alt: The two kidneys sit at the top, each joined by a ureter to the bladder below, with an arrow out of the bladder to the outside of the body.
diagram.caption: The path of urine from the kidneys to the outside.

cases.label: The path of urine

reveal.text: The nephrons do the filtering. After that the urine only travels, down the ureters, into storage and out. How much is filtered and how much returns comes next.
The kidneys filter a very large volume and return nearly all of it. The next screen puts numbers on both.

lead.text: About a litre of the 5 litres of blood the heart pumps each minute at rest passes through the kidneys, and from it the two kidneys together form filtrate at a rate called the **glomerular filtration rate**, or GFR. On average it is about 125 mL a minute in males (with a range of 90 to 140) and 105 mL a minute in females (80 to 125), which comes to about 180 litres a day in males and 150 litres in females.

Very little of that leaves the body. About **99 percent of the filtrate is returned to the circulation** by **reabsorption**, so that only about 1 to 2 litres of urine are produced in a day. Urine is therefore the small remainder of a very large filtration.

afterFigure.text: The figure draws the male day to scale, and the part left as urine is a sliver of the whole bar, which is the point of the arrangement. The kidneys can filter generously because almost everything is taken back, and what they let go can be adjusted.

diagram.alt: A bar for 180 litres of filtrate, shown in three views: the whole bar filtered, 99 percent of it returning to the blood, and the final 1 percent left as 1.8 litres of urine.
diagram.caption: A male's day of filtrate, drawn to scale. Use the buttons to follow it.

steps.headline: Find the daily urine from a filtration rate of 125 mL a minute, with 99 percent reabsorbed.

workedSteps.text: A day has 24 hours of 60 minutes each.
Multiply the rate by the minutes in a day to get the filtrate in millilitres.
There are 1,000 mL in a litre, so divide by 1,000.
Ninety-nine percent is reabsorbed, so 1 percent is left to leave as urine.
That is 1.8 litres a day, which sits inside the textbook's 1 to 2 litres.

steps.headline: Find the daily urine for a female whose kidneys form 105 mL of filtrate a minute, with 99 percent reabsorbed.

workedSteps.text: In a day of 1,440 minutes the filtrate is 105 × 1,440 = 151,200 mL, or 151.2 litres, which the textbook rounds to about 150 litres.
Ninety-nine percent is reabsorbed. Work out the urine from 150 litres of filtrate.
As for the male figures, the result falls inside the usual 1 to 2 litres a day.

lead.text: How much of the filtered water is recovered is not fixed, and a hormone sets it. In the **collecting ducts**, which carry the nearly finished urine through the kidney, **ADH** causes water channels called **aquaporins** to be inserted into the membrane of the cells lining the duct. With the channels in place, water is pulled out of the duct by osmosis, through the surrounding tissue and into nearby capillaries, so less water is left in the urine and the urine is more concentrated.

With less ADH, *fewer* channels are inserted and less water is recovered, which leaves the urine dilute. ADH therefore works by changing the number of channels, and the volume of water recovered or lost changes with it.

afterFigure.text: That adjustment is how the kidneys help to regulate blood osmolarity, blood pressure and the concentration of the urine. It does not follow the amount drunk directly: ADH responds to the body's need to recover water, so less is released when the blood is dilute and more when the body is short of water.
