reveal.text: The effect follows the channels: fewer channels, less water recovered, more water in the urine. More ADH does the opposite.

lead.text: ADH is one of three major hormones that influence total body water, the others being aldosterone and ANH. Blood loss and dehydration both deplete body fluid, and the body has to preserve both the volume of fluid and its concentration, because blood volume helps to maintain enough blood pressure.

**The fastest responses do not involve the kidney.** **Vasoconstriction**, the narrowing of blood vessels, can act *within seconds* of a drop in pressure. Thirst mechanisms are activated as well, to replace water lost through breathing, evaporation and urination, and the hormonal mechanisms act mainly on the kidney to recover volume while keeping the concentration of body fluids normal.

Cleansing the blood and ridding the body of wastes are the kidneys' best-known jobs, and the urinary system does more. The kidneys *share* the regulation of pH with the lungs and the buffers in the blood, and they share the regulation of blood pressure with the heart and blood vessels.

They also make **erythropoietin**, usually shortened to EPO, which stimulates the production of red blood cells: 85 percent of the body's EPO comes from the kidneys. The kidneys also carry out the final step in making vitamin D, converting calcidiol to calcitriol, which is the active form.

reveal.text: EPO links the kidneys to the blood itself. The kidneys do their best-known work on the blood, and they also help to decide how many red cells it carries.

lead.text: MedlinePlus says that **most kidney diseases attack the nephrons**, and since the nephrons do the filtering, the damage may leave the kidneys unable to remove wastes. Causes can include genetic problems, injuries and medicines. **Chronic kidney disease** damages the nephrons slowly, over several years.
The same summary lists three things that raise the risk of kidney disease: having diabetes, having high blood pressure, and having a close family member with kidney disease.

afterFigure.text: These are statements about *groups* of people, so they cannot say whether any one person has or will develop kidney disease. A doctor, nurse or pharmacist is the person to ask about your own health, and the next lessons return to both diabetes and blood pressure.

lead.text: Take the same day of 180 litres of filtrate and change one number.

reveal.text: A change of one percentage point in reabsorption doubles the urine. The kidneys adjust the fraction returned, and a small change in a large flow is a large change in what is left.

lessons.orientation: Follow a day's filtrate through the kidneys, find the urine volume, and see how ADH changes it.
lessons.nextAction: Describe an action potential from a voltage graph and follow a signal across a synapse.

blocks.text: Your kidneys form about 125 mL of filtrate a minute from the blood passing through them, which adds up to about 180 litres over a day in males, yet the urine you pass in that time is a small part of it. Almost everything filtered has to be taken back into the blood, and the balance between what returns and what is let go is how the body controls its water.

The same organs also help to control blood pressure and the making of red blood cells, and they are the target of a group of diseases that damage their filters. Following one day's numbers through shows how those jobs fit together.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to follow a day's filtrate through the kidneys, work out the urine left when 99 percent is reabsorbed, and say how ADH makes the urine dilute or concentrated.
intro.whyItMatters: Knowing what the filters do makes the listed risks for kidney disease easier to follow. It is general background, not advice about anyone's health.

recap.keyIdea: The kidneys filter about 180 litres a day and reabsorb about 99 percent of it, and ADH sets how much water is recovered, which decides whether the urine is dilute or concentrated.

blocks.text: The nephrons filter the blood and almost everything filtered returns to it, which leaves 1 to 2 litres of urine to travel through the ureters to the bladder. ADH changes the number of water channels in the collecting ducts, and with them the amount of water recovered, while the kidneys also help to regulate pH and blood pressure, make most of the body's erythropoietin and finish activating vitamin D.
Diabetes, high blood pressure and a close family member with kidney disease are the risk factors MedlinePlus lists.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson moves to nerves, where a signal is a voltage change across a membrane.

lessons.title: Nerves and senses

lead.text: A nerve cell keeps different concentrations of ions on the two sides of its membrane, and sodium (Na+) is about ten times more concentrated outside the cell than inside it. At rest the voltage just inside the membrane, measured against just outside, is −70 mV, and this value is called the **resting potential**.

When a channel for sodium opens, sodium ions rush into the cell, driven largely by the concentration difference. Each ion carries a positive charge, so the inside becomes *less* negative and the voltage moves toward zero. A change of this kind, in which the membrane potential moves toward zero, is called **depolarisation**.

The voltage does not stop at zero. By the time the membrane reaches +30 mV, other voltage-gated channels are opening, and these are specific for the potassium ion (K+). A concentration difference acts on potassium as well, so potassium starts to leave the cell and takes its positive charge with it, and the voltage begins to move back toward the resting value of −70 mV. This is called **repolarisation**.

afterFigure.text: Read as a graph, an **action potential** has three stages: a rest at −70 mV, a rise to about +30 mV as sodium enters, and a fall back toward −70 mV as potassium leaves. The size of the rise is found by subtracting the resting value from the peak.

diagram.alt: A voltage against time graph with gridlines at +30 mV, 0 mV and −70 mV. The line is flat at −70, rises steeply to +30, falls back and is flat again. One stage is highlighted in each view.

reveal.text: The rise from −70 mV to +30 mV is 100 mV. A negative starting value makes the distance larger than the peak alone suggests.

lead.text: The action potential runs along the **axon**, the long fibre of the nerve cell, to the axon terminals, where one cell passes its signal to the next at a junction called a **synapse**. At the terminal, voltage-gated calcium channels (Ca2+) open in the membrane of the synaptic end bulb. Calcium ions then enter, attach to proteins on the outside of the vesicles that hold **neurotransmitter**, and help the vesicles to merge with the membrane.
The merged vesicles release their neurotransmitter by exocytosis into the **synaptic cleft**, the small gap between the two cells, and the neurotransmitter binds to receptors on the next cell.

afterFigure.text: What crosses the gap is therefore a *chemical*, which is why the figure shows molecules and not a spark. The voltage signal along the cell and the chemical signal across the gap are two different forms of the same message.

diagram.alt: Two cells separated by a narrow gap. In four views, an action potential reaches the first cell's terminal, calcium channels open, vesicles release neurotransmitter into the gap, and neurotransmitter binds receptors on the second cell.
diagram.caption: The four steps at a chemical synapse. Use the buttons to step through them.

reveal.text: The order matters because each step makes the next one possible. Without calcium entering, the vesicles do not merge, and without release, nothing is there to bind.

lead.text: A signal has to start somewhere. Stimuli in the environment activate specialised receptor cells in the peripheral nervous system, and different types of stimuli are sensed by different types of receptor cells. A mechanical stimulus, light or a chemical changes the membrane potential of the receptor cell, and this conversion of a stimulus into a change in membrane potential is called **transduction**.
Receptor cells can be sorted in three ways: by cell type, by position in relation to the stimuli they sense, and by function, which means how the stimulus is transduced.

reveal.text: The arm withdraws without waiting for anything more elaborate. The textbook's example puts the first meeting in the spinal cord.

lead.text: The basic withdrawal reflex has three parts. The **sensory input** is the painful stimulus, the **central processing** is a synapse in the spinal cord, and the **motor output** is the activation of a ventral motor neuron that makes the biceps brachii contract. Together they form a **reflex arc**.
The picture can be made more complete. A collateral branch of the sensory axon inhibits another ventral horn motor neuron, so that the triceps brachii does not contract and slow the withdrawal down.

afterFigure.text: Every step of the arc uses ideas you have *already* met: the receptor transduces the stimulus, an action potential carries it, and a synapse passes it on.

lead.text: Many [[axons|The long fibre of a nerve cell, along which the action potential runs. Met in 'The chemical synapse'.]] are wrapped in **myelin**, an insulation around the axon. In multiple sclerosis, or MS, the antibodies produced by lymphocytes (a type of white blood cell) mark myelin as something that should not be in the body, which makes MS an example of an **autoimmune disease**. The result is inflammation and the destruction of myelin in the central nervous system.

As the insulation around the axons is destroyed, scarring becomes obvious, and sclerosis means hardening of tissue, which is what a scar is. Multiple scars are found in the white matter of the brain and spinal cord. The symptoms include loss of control of the muscles and of organs such as the bladder.

afterFigure.text: The disease acts on the signalling cells and *not* on the muscles themselves, so the loss of control follows from disrupted signals. Nothing here can help you recognise it in yourself or anyone else, and a doctor is the person to ask about any symptom.

reveal.text: MS is an attack on the insulation of the signalling cells, so the muscles lose control through the nerves and are not diseased themselves.

lead.text: Smell is also a sense that starts with receptor cells. Loss of the sense of smell can leave food tasting bland, and a person with an impaired sense of smell may need more spice and seasoning for food to be tasted.

The ability of olfactory neurons to replace themselves decreases with age, which leads to age-related loss of smell and explains why some elderly people salt their food more than younger people do. The textbook adds that **this increased sodium intake can increase blood volume and [[blood pressure|The pressure of blood on the walls of the vessels. Met in 'Blood vessels and blood pressure'.]]**, raising the risk of cardiovascular disease.

afterFigure.text: The word is *can*: the textbook describes a tendency across people and does not say that it happens to everyone with a weaker sense of smell.

lead.text: Apply what you know about receptors and about blood volume to a case from the textbook.

reveal.text: Each link in the chain is a change that follows from the one before. A sense that seems unrelated to blood pressure reaches it through habits around food.

lessons.orientation: Read an action potential from its voltage values, follow a signal across a synapse and through a reflex, and say what damage to myelin does.
lessons.nextAction: Name the hormones that hold blood glucose steady and say what goes wrong in type 2 diabetes.

blocks.text: A nerve cell at rest holds the inside of its membrane at about −70 millivolts relative to the outside. When the cell sends a signal that voltage climbs to about +30 mV and falls back again, and this brief change is what travels along the cell. It is produced by ions moving through channels in the membrane.

Between one nerve cell and the next the signal changes form: it crosses a small gap as a chemical. The same pieces, a receptor, a voltage change and a gap, make up a reflex such as pulling a hand away from heat, and damage to the insulation around nerve cells, as in multiple sclerosis, disrupts the signalling.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read an action potential from its voltage values, order the events at a synapse and in a reflex, and say what damage to myelin does to signalling.
intro.whyItMatters: Pulling a hand from heat and noticing a smell both rest on these signals. This is general background, not a guide to any symptom.

recap.keyIdea: A nerve signal is a brief rise and fall of membrane voltage, from −70 mV to about +30 mV and back, which crosses from cell to cell as a chemical at a synapse.

blocks.text: Sodium entering drives the rise and potassium leaving drives the fall, a swing of 100 mV. At a synapse, calcium entry releases neurotransmitter into the cleft, and a reflex arc joins sensory input, processing in the spinal cord and motor output.
When myelin is destroyed, as in multiple sclerosis, signalling along the axons is disrupted, and the textbook also links the loss of smell with age to salting food more.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson moves from nerves to hormones, which carry signals through the blood.

lessons.title: Hormones and blood sugar

lead.text: A **hormone** is a chemical messenger released into the blood. It may travel throughout the body in the bloodstream, but it affects the activity *only* of its **target cells**, which are the cells with receptors for that particular hormone. When the hormone binds to its receptor, a chain of events starts inside the cell and leads to the target cell's response.
These responses help to regulate reproduction, growth and the development of tissues, metabolism, fluid and electrolyte balance, sleep and many other functions.

afterFigure.text: Of these, the control of blood glucose has the clearest numbers, and it is the example that follows.

diagram.caption: One hormone in the blood, and three cells. Use the buttons to compare what reaches them with what responds.

reveal.text: Delivery is the same for every cell, and the receptor decides the response. The same rule applies to every hormone in the body.
The hormones come as a pair, one for a level above the range and one for a level below it. The next screen gives the range and the numbers.

lead.text: Glucose is required for cellular respiration and is the preferred fuel for all body cells. The body gets it from the breakdown of carbohydrate-containing foods and drinks, and glucose that cells do not immediately take up can be stored by the liver and muscles as glycogen, or converted to triglycerides and stored in adipose tissue. Hormones regulate both the storage and the use of glucose, and [[receptors|Proteins on or in a cell that a hormone binds to. Met in 'Hormones and target cells'.]] in the pancreas sense the level in the blood, after which pancreatic cells secrete **insulin** or **glucagon**.

The concentration of glucose in the blood is tightly maintained between **70 mg/dL and 100 mg/dL**, where mg/dL means milligrams in a decilitre, a tenth of a litre. Many laboratory reports use millimoles per litre (mmol/L) instead, and the same range is about 3.9 to 5.6 mmol/L, because one mmol/L is about 18 mg/dL. If the level rises above the range, insulin is released and stimulates body cells to remove glucose from the blood. If it drops below the range, glucagon is released and stimulates body cells to release glucose into the blood.

afterFigure.text: Each hormone is switched off as the level moves back into the range, which is why the control corrects in both directions and then settles. A range like this describes how the body regulates glucose in general, and the target that suits any one person is for that person's clinician to set.

diagram.alt: A four-step loop. In the first view blood glucose is above 100 mg/dL, the pancreas senses it, insulin is released and body cells take up glucose. In the second the glucose is below 70 mg/dL, glucagon is released and body cells release glucose into the blood. In both a green arrow shows the level returning toward the range.
diagram.caption: The blood glucose control loop in its two cases. Use the buttons to switch between them.

reveal.text: The loop is a response to a change, and it ends when the change has been undone. Glucose that is not needed at once goes into storage.

steps.headline: A reading taken just after a meal is reported as 6.5 mmol/L. Compare it with the range and say which hormone responds.

workedSteps.text: The range is given in mg/dL, so convert the reading by multiplying by about 18.
Compare 117 with the range of 70 to 100 mg/dL.
The reading is above the range, so insulin is released and stimulates body cells to remove glucose from the blood.
As the cells take up glucose, the level falls back toward the range.

steps.headline: A reading is reported as 3.0 mmol/L. Compare it with the range and say which hormone responds.

workedSteps.text: The range is in mg/dL, so convert the reading before comparing.
Compare that value with the range of 70 to 100 mg/dL. It is below 70, so the level is below the range.
A level below the range releases glucagon, which stimulates body cells to release glucose into the blood.

lead.text: Type 2 diabetes accounts for approximately **95 percent of all cases** of diabetes. It is acquired, and lifestyle factors such as poor diet, inactivity and pre-diabetes greatly increase a person's risk. About 80 to 90 percent of people with type 2 diabetes are overweight or obese, and WHO names being overweight, not getting enough exercise and genetics among the contributing factors.

In type 2 diabetes the cells become resistant to the effects of insulin, which is called **insulin resistance**. In response the pancreas increases its insulin secretion, but over time the **beta cells** that make insulin become exhausted.

afterFigure.text: Insulin is therefore present at the start, and it is the *response* of the cells that is weak. Only later does the supply itself fall.

diagram.alt: Three sketches of a bar for insulin made by the pancreas, an arrow, and a box for body cells. Healthy: a medium bar and cells that take up glucose. Resistant: a tall bar and cells that respond weakly. Over time: a short bar and cells that respond weakly.
diagram.caption: Insulin made and the cells' response in three stages. Use the buttons to follow the change.

reveal.text: A share of this size tells you where most of the people are, so the factors behind type 2 diabetes touch the large majority of cases.

lead.text: Two of the early signs of diabetes are **excessive urination and excessive thirst**, and they show how out-of-control glucose affects the kidneys. The kidneys are responsible for filtering glucose from the blood, and *excessive* blood glucose draws water into the urine. As a result the person eliminates an abnormally large quantity of sweet urine.

Using body water to dilute the urine leaves the body dehydrated, so the person is unusually and continually thirsty. The person may also feel persistent hunger, because the body cells are unable to access the glucose in the bloodstream.

afterFigure.text: This links back to the kidneys: water follows glucose into the [[filtrate|The fluid the kidneys filter out of the blood. Met in 'Kidneys and water balance'.]], and the body loses water it needs.

reveal.text: Each step follows from the one before it, and thirst is the last link. The reasoning runs through the kidneys.

lead.text: WHO says that over time type 2 diabetes can cause serious damage to the body, especially to the nerves and blood vessels, and that it is often preventable. **Lifestyle changes are the best way to prevent or delay it**, and WHO lists *four* measures: reaching and keeping a healthy body weight, staying physically active with at least 150 minutes of moderate exercise each week, eating a healthy diet that avoids sugar and saturated fat, and not smoking tobacco.
Early diagnosis matters because it helps to prevent the worst effects, and WHO says the best way to detect diabetes early is to have regular check-ups and blood tests with a healthcare provider.

afterFigure.text: These are general public-health statements. What suits you, including any test or target, is for your own healthcare provider to say.

lead.text: Apply the loop to a changed case.

reveal.text: The pancreas works harder first and fails later. That order is why a high output early on is not a sign that the system is healthy.

lessons.orientation: See how hormones reach only their target cells, how insulin and glucagon hold blood glucose in range, and what goes wrong in type 2 diabetes.
lessons.nextAction: Separate the innate and adaptive immune responses and explain why a second exposure is stronger.

blocks.text: Glucose is the preferred fuel of every body cell, and its concentration in the blood is held tightly between 70 mg/dL and 100 mg/dL, which is about 3.9 to 5.6 mmol/L in the units many laboratory reports use. A meal sends the level up, yet it returns to the range because the pancreas releases a chemical messenger that moves it back, and a second messenger does the same job in the other direction when the level drops.

When this control fails, as it does in diabetes, the kidneys are affected, which is why thirst and passing a large amount of urine can be among the first signs. The first idea needed is how a chemical messenger that travels everywhere in the blood acts on only some cells.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say how insulin and glucagon hold blood glucose in range, convert a reading between mg/dL and mmol/L, and describe type 2 diabetes and the WHO's list for preventing it.
intro.whyItMatters: Blood glucose numbers appear on laboratory reports and in health news. This is general background, and targets for any person are set by their clinician.

recap.keyIdea: Insulin lowers and glucagon raises blood glucose, which keeps it between 70 and 100 mg/dL (about 3.9 to 5.6 mmol/L), and in type 2 diabetes the cells resist insulin until the beta cells become exhausted.

blocks.text: A hormone acts only on cells with receptors for it, and the pancreas releases insulin when the glucose level is above the range and glucagon when it is below. High glucose in the filtrate draws water into the urine, which explains the thirst and frequent urination that are early signs of diabetes.
WHO lists a healthy body weight, at least 150 minutes of moderate exercise a week, a healthy diet that avoids sugar and saturated fat, and not smoking as ways to prevent or delay type 2 diabetes.

recap.nextHook: The last lesson turns to the immune system, which uses memory in a way that vaccines borrow.

lessons.title: The immune system and vaccines

lead.text: The immune system can be divided into two overlapping mechanisms for destroying pathogens. The **innate immune response** is relatively rapid but nonspecific, and so is not always effective. The **adaptive immune response** is slower to develop during an initial infection with a pathogen, but it is *highly specific* and effective at attacking a wide variety of pathogens.

afterFigure.text: The two overlap, and the figure shows the order in which they act on a new infection. The adaptive response is the one followed from here, because that is where the memory lies.

diagram.alt: Two horizontal bars on a time axis. The innate bar starts early and is labelled not specific. The adaptive bar starts later and is labelled specific. One bar is highlighted in each view.
diagram.caption: The order in which the two responses act on a new infection. Use the buttons to highlight each.

reveal.text: A second meeting with a pathogen gives a quicker, larger response than the first. The next screens say what makes it so.

lead.text: B cells are immune cells that function mainly by producing **antibodies**. An antibody is a protein that binds specifically to a pathogen-associated molecule called an **antigen**, which is a chemical structure on the surface of a pathogen. When a B cell is activated by binding to its antigen, it differentiates into a cell that secretes a soluble form of its surface antibodies, and these activated B cells are known as **plasma cells**.

afterFigure.text: The word *specific* is the important one. A given antibody answers a given antigen, which is what the adaptive response adds to the nonspecific innate one.

lead.text: On a first exposure to a pathogen the adaptive response is called the **primary response**, and it is slow to develop. When the same pathogen is met again, a **secondary response** is generated, which is stronger and faster than the primary one.

The secondary response often eliminates a pathogen before it can cause significant tissue damage or any symptoms. Without symptoms there is no disease, and the person is not even aware of the infection. This secondary response is the basis of **immunological memory**, which protects us from getting diseases repeatedly from the same pathogen.

afterFigure.text: On a graph of antibody level against time since exposure, the secondary response is the curve that begins to rise *sooner* and climbs *higher*. The curves in the figure are sketches of those shapes and carry no measured values.

diagram.alt: A graph of antibody level against time since exposure. The first-exposure curve rises late to a low peak. The second-exposure curve rises early to a higher peak. The third view draws both together.
diagram.caption: Antibody curves for a first and a second exposure to the same pathogen. Use the buttons to compare.

reveal.text: A response that is strong and fast enough can end an infection before it does damage. That is the property a vaccine aims to use.

lead.text: A **vaccine** is a killed or weakened pathogen, or its components, that when given to a healthy individual leads to the development of immunological memory, a weakened primary immune response, *without* causing much in the way of symptoms. With a vaccine, a person can avoid the damage from disease that results from the first exposure to the pathogen and still gain the protection of immunological memory.

The textbook calls the advent of vaccines one of the major medical advances of the twentieth century. It says that vaccines led to the eradication of smallpox and to the control of many infectious diseases, including polio, measles and whooping cough.

afterFigure.text: A vaccine therefore borrows what the primary response builds and leaves out most of the symptoms of a real first infection.

reveal.text: The key is that the body builds the memory itself. What the vaccine supplies is a safe first meeting with the pathogen's parts.

lead.text: [[Immunological memory|The stronger, faster response to a pathogen the body has met before. Met in 'The second exposure'.]] protects against the pathogen the body has met, and a pathogen can change. The surface molecules of viruses **mutate continuously**, and viruses such as influenza change enough each year that the flu vaccine for one year *may not* protect against the flu common to the next. New vaccine formulations must be derived for each flu season.

afterFigure.text: The textbook describes mutation as another method of immune evasion, which means a way for a pathogen to avoid being recognised.

reveal.text: Memory is about what the body has met, and the influenza virus keeps changing what it presents. So a new formulation is needed each season.

lead.text: Public-health bodies report how many people have been vaccinated as a **coverage** figure, the share of a group that has received a dose. WHO reports that by the end of 2025, 84 percent of children had received one dose of a measles-containing vaccine by their second birthday, and 77 percent had received two doses. By then 192 Member States had included a second dose of measles vaccine in their national immunization schedules.
Measles is a highly contagious disease caused by a virus. It usually causes a high fever and rash, and it can lead to blindness, encephalitis or death.

afterFigure.text: Each figure answers a narrow question: **which dose, which children and which year**. A figure can also be read from the other side. If 84 percent had a first dose, then 16 in every 100 had not. The 77 percent for two doses is a *separate* measurement and is read on its own. A published schedule lists the vaccines a health service offers; the NHS, for example, lists the flu vaccine for people at higher risk from flu, including adults aged 65 and over, and for most children. Your own country's health service publishes its schedule, and it is the place to find what applies to you.

steps.headline: Out of 2,500 children, 84 percent had a first dose of measles vaccine by their second birthday. How many had not?

workedSteps.text: The coverage figure is the share who had a dose, so the share who had not is the rest of 100 percent.
Write 16 percent as a decimal.
Multiply by the number of children.
So 400 of the 2,500 children had not had a first dose.

steps.headline: In a district of 2,000 children, 84 percent had a first dose of measles vaccine. How many had, and how many had not?

workedSteps.text: Write the coverage figure of 84 percent as a decimal.
Multiply by the number of children to find how many had a dose.
The others had not, so subtract that from the 2,000.

lead.text: Apply the figure to a case outside the lesson.

reveal.text: A coverage figure always has a dose, a group and a year behind it. A number reported without them cannot be compared with another.

lessons.orientation: Separate innate from adaptive immunity, read an antibody graph, say what a vaccine is, and work with a coverage figure.
lessons.nextAction: Use the whole course to read health information: name the system behind each figure and what it controls.

blocks.text: When the body meets a pathogen for the first time, the person may become ill while the immune system responds. A second meeting with the same pathogen often passes unnoticed: the person has no symptoms at all and is not even aware of the infection. The difference lies in the immune system's memory, and the preparations given before an infection to prevent illness are designed to make use of it.
The immune system is made of two overlapping mechanisms that work at different speeds, and the memory belongs to one of them.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to sort features into innate and adaptive, read an antibody graph for a first and a second exposure, say what a vaccine is, and work out a number from a coverage figure.
intro.whyItMatters: Vaccination figures turn up in the news and in public-health reports. This explains what they say and does not advise anyone about vaccines.

recap.keyIdea: A vaccine gives the adaptive immune system a first meeting with a pathogen that causes little in the way of symptoms, so the stronger and faster secondary response is ready if the real pathogen arrives.

blocks.text: The innate response is rapid but nonspecific, while the adaptive response is slower at first and highly specific, with B cells making antibodies that bind antigens. On a second exposure the antibody curve rises sooner and higher, which is the basis of immunological memory, and the flu vaccine is changed each season because the virus's surface molecules mutate.

A coverage figure such as WHO's 84 percent for a first dose of measles vaccine answers a narrow question about a dose, a group and a year, and its remainder, 16 in every 100, is read from the same figure.

questions.prompt: A muscle cell and a nerve cell are taken from the same adult. Which statement fits what the textbook says about cell types like these?
hints: Think about what the passage says the 200 or more cell types have in common, and what they differ in.
One option says the cells are the same kind and one says they differ inside. Check each against the screen.

acceptedIdeas: They share essentially the same internal structures but differ in shape and function
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They share essentially the same internal structures but differ in shape and function

questions.onCorrect: Cells with the same internal structures can still differ in shape and function, which is how one body holds at least 200 cell types.

misconceptions.feedback: Descent from one egg does not make cells the same kind. Early cells differentiate, and the body ends up with at least 200 distinct cell types.
Shape varies enormously between cell types, and it is one of the main ways they differ.
The internal structures are essentially the same from one cell type to another. The differences lie in shape and function.

choices.label: They share essentially the same internal structures but differ in shape and function
They are the same kind of cell, because both descend from one fertilised egg
They share one shape, set by the egg, and differ only in the job they do
They differ in their internal structures, because each job needs different parts

questions.prompt: A sample from the inside of an airway shows flat sheets of tightly packed cells forming a layer along the passage. Which tissue category is this?
hints: Ask what the cells are doing in this sample: binding, contracting, signalling or covering a surface.
A passageway inside the body counts as a surface the tissue can line.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Epithelial

questions.onCorrect: Epithelium lines internal passageways as well as covering the outside of the body, so a lining sheet like this one is epithelial.

misconceptions.feedback: Connective tissue binds cells and organs together and supports them. A tightly packed sheet along a surface is the pattern of epithelium.
Muscle tissue is excitable and contracts to produce movement. It is not arranged as a sheet lining a passage.
Nervous tissue carries electrochemical signals. It is not arranged as a sheet lining a passage.

choices.label: Connective
Epithelial
Muscle
Nervous

questions.prompt: Which statement fits the textbook account of how cancer arises?
hints: Think about whether cancer starts inside the body or arrives from outside.
The passage says a regulation system directs cells to divide or stop.

acceptedIdeas: The signals that control division fail, so cells keep dividing
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The signals that control division fail, so cells keep dividing

questions.onCorrect: Cancer begins with the body's own cells when the controls on division fail, and the immune system often removes such cells.

misconceptions.feedback: Cancer starts from the body's own cells. The textbook describes a cell escaping its normal control system, not an outside cell arriving.
Loss of blood supply is not the textbook's account. It describes cells escaping the controls on division.
Stem cells can divide without limit as needed. The account of cancer is about too much division, not too little.

choices.label: A kind of cell the body never makes gets in from outside and takes over
The tissue loses its blood supply, so its cells turn abnormal and spread
The signals that control division fail, so cells keep dividing
Stem cells stop dividing altogether, so damaged cells are never replaced

questions.prompt: In a tissue, one cell's stop signals no longer work, while its advance signals still do. What is the likely effect on its division?
hints: The control system has two kinds of signal. Ask what the cell loses when one kind is gone.
Think about which outcome the textbook links to loss of cell cycle control.

acceptedIdeas: Nothing holds it back, so it may keep dividing when it should not
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Nothing holds it back, so it may keep dividing when it should not

questions.onCorrect: A cell that has lost its stop signal has lost part of the control system, which is the situation the textbook links to cancer.

misconceptions.feedback: Differentiation is a separate process from the control of division. Losing a stop signal does not make a cell specialise.
The passage says loss of control can lead to cancer, which is the opposite of cells dying out.
A stop signal is half of the control system. Without it, nothing holds the cell back once it has been told to advance.

choices.label: Nothing holds it back, so it may keep dividing when it should not
It becomes a specialised cell, because division can no longer proceed
It dies at once, because every cell needs a stop signal to survive
Nothing changes, because the advance signals still work as before

questions.prompt: Sort each job into the tissue category that does it.
hints: Start with the two excitable tissues: one contracts and one carries signals.
Of the other two, one forms sheets on surfaces and the other holds things together.
questions.onCorrect: Each tissue is defined by its job and by how its cells are arranged, so the same four categories cover every organ in the body.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Epithelial: lines a passageway, covers the outside. Connective: binds organs together, supports and protects. Muscle: contracts, provides movement. Nervous: carries impulses, communicates between regions.

items.label: Lines a passageway inside the body
items.explanation: Sheets of cells that line internal passageways are epithelium.

items.label: Binds organs together
items.explanation: Binding the cells and organs of the body together is the job of connective tissue.

items.label: Responds to stimulation by contracting
items.explanation: Muscle tissue is excitable and contracts to produce movement.

items.label: Carries nerve impulses
items.explanation: Nervous tissue propagates electrochemical signals as nerve impulses.

items.label: Covers the outside of the body
items.explanation: Epithelium covers exterior surfaces of the body.

items.label: Supports and protects other parts of the body
items.explanation: Protection and support are functions of connective tissue.

items.label: Provides the movement of the body and of the heart
items.explanation: Skeletal, smooth and cardiac muscle all contract to provide movement.

items.label: Communicates between different regions of the body
items.explanation: Nerve impulses communicate between different regions of the body.

questions.prompt: This is how a textbook separates two kinds of tumour. What decides whether a tumour counts as benign or malignant?

extracts.text: If the resulting tumor does not pose a threat to surrounding tissues, it is said to be benign and can usually be easily removed. If capable of damage, the tumor is considered malignant and the patient is diagnosed with cancer.
extracts.who: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, Chapter 3: The Cellular Level of Organization
extracts.when: in its section on the cell cycle and cancer
extracts.kind: A university-level textbook for students of anatomy and physiology

hints: Read the two sentences and find what each one says about surrounding tissues.
One option mentions size, one the immune system, one tissue type. Check whether the passage uses any of them.

acceptedIdeas: Whether it can damage the tissues around it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Whether it can damage the tissues around it

questions.onCorrect: A tumour that threatens nothing around it is benign, while one capable of damage is malignant, and the person is then diagnosed with cancer.

misconceptions.feedback: Size is not what the passage uses. It separates the two by whether the tumour can damage surrounding tissues.
The immune system comes earlier in the account, as one way such cells are removed. It does not decide how a tumour is classified.
The passage does not classify tumours by tissue type. It uses the threat to surrounding tissues.

choices.label: How large it has grown by the time it is found
Whether it can damage the tissues around it
Whether the immune system has noticed it
Which of the four tissue types it started in

questions.prompt: An unspecialised cell that can divide without limit as needed and can, under specific conditions, become a specialised cell is called a ___ cell.
hints: The answer is a single word that names this kind of cell.
It is the cell the screen compared with the specialised cells of a tissue.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: stem

questions.onCorrect: Stem cells keep up a supply of unspecialised cells and can give rise to specialised ones.

questions.prompt: Core temperature is held at about 36.5 to 37.5 degrees Celsius. A thermometer reading is 38.1 degrees Celsius. By how many degrees does it exceed the top of the range?
hints: Find the top of the range first.
The excess is measured from the top of the range, so use the larger of the two numbers, 37.5.
Subtract 37.5 from 38.1.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The top of the range is 37.5, and 38.1 - 37.5 = 0.6.

questions.onCorrect: The reading is 0.6 degrees above the top of the range, so a value is read against a range and not against one fixed number.

misconceptions.feedback: That measures from the bottom of the range, 36.5. The excess is measured from the top.
37.5 is the top of the range, the place to start. The question asks how far past it the reading is.

questions.prompt: A person stands in a very cold place and their core temperature falls below the set value. Which pair of responses does the hypothalamus start?
hints: Ask which responses make heat and which lose it.
A cold body needs to gain heat. Two of the four options include a response that loses it.

acceptedIdeas: Shivering, together with thyroid hormone raising heat production
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Shivering, together with thyroid hormone raising heat production

questions.onCorrect: Shivering and thyroid hormone both raise heat production, which pushes the temperature back up toward the range.

misconceptions.feedback: Both of these are responses to being too warm. They lose heat when the body needs to keep it.
More blood flowing to the skin lets heat escape through it, so it is the response to being too warm and would work against warming.
Sweating cools the skin as water evaporates, so it is the response to being too warm.

choices.label: Sweating, together with more blood flowing to the surface of the body
Shivering, together with more blood flowing to the surface of the body
Shivering, together with thyroid hormone raising heat production
Sweating, together with thyroid hormone raising energy use and heat production

questions.prompt: A student reads that glucocorticoid release is controlled by negative feedback and assumes the loop must be harmful. What does negative feedback mean in the textbook's account?
hints: Look at what happens to glucocorticoid secretion as its level in the blood rises.
The word negative names the direction of the response, and says nothing about whether the effect is good.

acceptedIdeas: Further release of a hormone is inhibited once its level is adequate
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Further release of a hormone is inhibited once its level is adequate

questions.onCorrect: Glucocorticoid release switches itself off as blood levels rise, which keeps the level within a narrow range.

misconceptions.feedback: Negative describes the direction of the response, which opposes the change. Negative feedback is the common way the body keeps values in a narrow range.
That describes positive feedback, which adds to the change instead of opposing it.
Negative feedback works all the time to hold a value in a narrow range, and illness comes when a value moves far out of range.

choices.label: A loop that harms the body by pushing a value out of its range
A loop in which the original release of a hormone causes more of it to be released
A loop that switches on only after illness has already begun
Further release of a hormone is inhibited once its level is adequate

questions.prompt: Blood pressure rises too high. Which pair of changes would bring it back down?
hints: Pressure depends on how much blood the heart pumps and on how freely the blood flows through the vessels.
To lower pressure, both changes have to point the same way.

acceptedIdeas: Cardiac output falls and the arterioles widen
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Cardiac output falls and the arterioles widen

questions.onCorrect: The reflex lowers cardiac output and widens the arterioles together, and the two changes combine to bring pressure down.

misconceptions.feedback: A rise in cardiac output pushes pressure up. It works against the widening of the arterioles, which lowers it.
Narrowing arterioles raise pressure. They work against the fall in cardiac output, which lowers it.
Both of these changes raise pressure, so this pair would push it further out of range.

choices.label: Cardiac output falls and the arterioles widen
Cardiac output rises and the arterioles widen
Cardiac output falls and the arterioles narrow
Cardiac output rises and the arterioles narrow

questions.prompt: In one loop, a change in a value triggers a response. What decides whether the loop is negative or positive feedback?
hints: Compare the oxytocin loop with the glucocorticoid loop: what does each response do to the change that started it?
The answer is about direction, and the other three options are about something else.

acceptedIdeas: Whether the response opposes the change or adds to it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Whether the response opposes the change or adds to it

questions.onCorrect: A negative loop opposes the change and holds a value in a narrow range, while a positive loop adds to it.

misconceptions.feedback: The sign of a loop describes what the response does to the change. Whether the effect is good or bad is a separate question.
Both kinds of loop are found with hormones, and the baroreceptor reflex is a negative loop that uses nerve signals.
Speed does not decide it. A loop is negative or positive by whether it opposes the change or adds to it.

choices.label: Whether the response is good for the body or harmful to it
Whether the response opposes the change or adds to it
Whether the loop uses a hormone and not a nerve signal
Whether the response follows the change quickly or slowly

questions.prompt: Blood pressure has risen too high. Put the steps of the baroreceptor reflex in the order they happen.
hints: Start with the change that sets the loop off and end with what the loop achieves.
The sensors report first, the control centre responds to the report, and the effectors act last.
questions.onCorrect: The sensors, control centre and effectors always act in this order, and the result opposes the change that started the sequence.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Pressure rises, the baroreceptors fire faster, the cardiovascular centre triggers the reflex, the nerve signals to the heart and arterioles change, output falls and the vessels widen, and pressure falls.

items: Blood pressure rises too high
The baroreceptors are stretched more tightly and fire at a higher rate
The cardiovascular centre receives the signal and triggers a reflex
Parasympathetic stimulation of the heart rises and sympathetic stimulation of the arterioles falls
Cardiac output falls and the arterioles widen
Blood pressure falls

questions.prompt: Sort each example into the kind of feedback it shows.
hints: Ask of each example whether the response opposes the change or adds to it.
Four of the five examples hold a value in a narrow range.
questions.onCorrect: Negative feedback is the usual pattern, and the oxytocin loop of childbirth is the textbook's example of the less common positive pattern.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sweating, shivering, glucocorticoid release easing off and the baroreceptor reflex are negative feedback. The oxytocin loop is positive feedback.

items.label: Sweating when the core temperature is too high
items.explanation: The response cools the body, so it opposes the rise.

items.label: Shivering when the core temperature falls below the set value
items.explanation: The response makes heat, so it opposes the fall.

items.label: Glucocorticoid release easing off as blood levels rise
items.explanation: Rising levels reduce further release, so the response opposes the change.

items.label: Oxytocin release that intensifies labour contractions
items.explanation: More oxytocin makes contractions stronger, which causes more oxytocin release, so the change is amplified until the birth.

items.label: Baroreceptors lowering a raised blood pressure
items.explanation: The reflex lowers pressure, so it opposes the rise.

questions.prompt: Which description of homeostasis matches the textbook's?
hints: The textbook's description has two key words: one says the state moves, the other says it has limits.
Check each option against the example of core temperature.

acceptedIdeas: A dynamic state of balance within parameters that are compatible with life
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A dynamic state of balance within parameters that are compatible with life

questions.onCorrect: Homeostasis keeps values within limits compatible with life, and a value that moves far enough out of its range leads to illness.

misconceptions.feedback: Homeostasis is dynamic. Values move about inside a range, as core temperature does between 36.5 and 37.5 degrees Celsius.
That describes positive feedback. Homeostasis is mostly kept by negative feedback, which opposes the change.
The surroundings can be very different while the core temperature stays in its range, so they are not what homeostasis names.

choices.label: A state in which every measurement in the body stays at one fixed value for life
A response that always makes the change that set it off larger
A dynamic state of balance within parameters that are compatible with life
The temperature of the air and the surfaces around the body

questions.prompt: On the surface of a bone, one cell is dissolving old, unnecessary bone to release calcium. Which cell is it, and what is the process called?
hints: Decide first whether the cell is building bone or breaking it down.
Osteoclasts and osteoblasts have opposite jobs, and resorption is the word for breakdown.

acceptedIdeas: An osteoclast, carrying out bone resorption
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An osteoclast, carrying out bone resorption

questions.onCorrect: Osteoclasts keep breaking old bone down while osteoblasts keep forming new bone, and the balance between them reshapes bone.

misconceptions.feedback: An osteoblast forms new bone. Breaking bone down is the osteoclast's job.
Osteoclasts break bone down, and that process is resorption. Formation is what osteoblasts do.
Osteoblasts do form bone, but the cell in the question is dissolving it.

choices.label: An osteoblast, carrying out bone resorption
An osteoclast, carrying out bone formation
An osteoblast, carrying out bone formation
An osteoclast, carrying out bone resorption

questions.prompt: Osteoporosis is described as a disease in which:
hints: Think about the balance on the figure and which side is ahead in this disease.
One option describes a different disease, and one has the two cells' jobs swapped.

acceptedIdeas: bone is broken down faster than it is formed, so bone mass falls
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: bone is broken down faster than it is formed, so bone mass falls

questions.onCorrect: Resorption outrunning formation is the textbook's definition, and it is a common occurrence as the body ages.

misconceptions.feedback: The roles are swapped here. Osteoclasts break bone down and osteoblasts form it.
The textbook's account is about the balance between breakdown and formation of bone, and says nothing of calcium moving into muscle.
That describes Paget's disease, where new bone is made in a disorderly way. Osteoporosis is a net loss of bone mass.

choices.label: bone is broken down faster than it is formed, so bone mass falls
osteoblasts break bone down faster than osteoclasts can form new bone
calcium is stored in muscle instead of bone, so the bones thin
new bone is formed haphazardly by overactive osteoclasts

questions.prompt: A person's leg looks thinner after weeks in a cast. According to the textbook, what has happened inside the muscle?
hints: The textbook says one thing about muscle fibres stays fixed and one thing changes with use.
Strength is directly related to the amount of myofibrils and sarcomeres inside each fibre.

acceptedIdeas: Each fibre has lost sarcomeres and myofibrils, but the fibres remain
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each fibre has lost sarcomeres and myofibrils, but the fibres remain

questions.onCorrect: Disuse removes sarcomeres and myofibrils from each fibre, and the number of fibres, which is genetically determined, stays the same.

misconceptions.feedback: The textbook describes atrophy as a loss of sarcomeres and myofibrils, and says the number of muscle fibres does not change.
Muscle does not change into tendon. Atrophy is a loss of contracting machinery inside fibres that remain.
The textbook gives a limb in a cast as a common example of atrophied muscle, so use and disuse do change a muscle.

choices.label: Many of the fibres have died and been replaced by fat tissue in the leg
The fibres have shortened and turned into tendon tissue over the weeks
Each fibre has lost sarcomeres and myofibrils, but the fibres remain
Nothing has changed in the muscle, because fibre numbers fall only with age

questions.prompt: Why does the working multiply the baseline by 0.20 instead of adding 20 to it?
hints: A percentage of something is a share of that thing.
Check what 20 percent of 40 comes to, and compare it with adding 20.

acceptedIdeas: A percentage increase is a share of the baseline, and 20 percent of 40 is 8
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A percentage increase is a share of the baseline, and 20 percent of 40 is 8

questions.onCorrect: The increase is a share of the baseline, so the same percentage gives different counts when the baseline differs.

misconceptions.feedback: A percentage increase is a share of the baseline, which can be any number, so it is not a count out of 100.
Adding 20 gives a number of 60, which is above both ends of the range, so it is not the upper end.
The baseline is what the percentage is taken of, so without it the increase cannot be found.

choices.label: Percentages are always turned into a count out of 100 before they are used in sums
A percentage increase is a share of the baseline, and 20 percent of 40 is 8
Adding 20 would give the upper end of the range and not the lower end
The baseline is not needed to work out a percentage increase

questions.prompt: The baseline is 60 in 1,000 and a 20 percent increase adds 12. What is the lower end of the range, in deaths per 1,000?
hints: The range starts from the baseline and adds the increase.
The increase is the 12 already found.
Add 12 to 60.
questions.onCorrect: A 20 percent increase on a baseline of 60 gives 72 per 1,000, the lower end of the range.

misconceptions.feedback: 12 is the increase alone. The range is the baseline plus the increase.
That adds 20 to the baseline, as if 20 percent meant 20 extra. The increase is 20 percent of 60.

questions.prompt: A 30 percent increase on the baseline of 60 adds 18. What is the upper end of the range, in deaths per 1,000?
hints: The upper end comes from the larger percentage.
The increase is the 18 already found.
Add 18 to the baseline of 60.
questions.onCorrect: A 30 percent increase on a baseline of 60 gives 78 per 1,000, so the range is 72 to 78.

misconceptions.feedback: 18 is the increase alone. The range is the baseline plus the increase.
That adds 30 to the baseline, as if 30 percent meant 30 extra. The increase is 30 percent of 60.

questions.prompt: A headline says that insufficiently active people have a 25 percent higher risk of death. A reader concludes that 25 of every 100 insufficiently active people will die. What is wrong with that reading?
hints: Ask what the 25 percent is a percentage of.
If the baseline risk were 2 in 100, would 25 extra deaths in 100 be possible?

acceptedIdeas: A 25 percent rise is relative to the baseline risk, so it is not a count of 25 in 100
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A 25 percent rise is relative to the baseline risk, so it is not a count of 25 in 100

questions.onCorrect: A relative increase is taken of the baseline, so 25 percent more than a small baseline is a small number of extra deaths.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats a relative increase as percentage points. The increase is 25 percent of whatever the baseline risk was.
A figure like this compares two groups and does not predict what happens to one person.
The figure compares people who are insufficiently active with people who are sufficiently active, as groups.

choices.label: A 25 percent rise is relative to the baseline risk, so it is not a count of 25 in 100
Nothing is wrong, since a 25 percent increase means 25 extra deaths in every 100
Risk figures describe single people, so the 25 percent applies to each of them alone
The percentage applies only to people who are very inactive, and not to the whole group

questions.prompt: Suppose, with invented figures, that 50 in 1,000 sufficiently active adults die during a study period. The WHO says that insufficiently active people have a 20 to 30 percent increased risk of death compared with sufficiently active people. What is the highest number of deaths per 1,000 you would expect in a comparable insufficiently active group?
hints: The highest number comes from the larger percentage, 30.
Find 30 percent of the baseline of 50 first.
Add that increase to the baseline.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 30 percent of 50 is 15, and 50 + 15 = 65.

questions.onCorrect: The range is 60 to 65 per 1,000, which is 10 to 15 more than the baseline and not 20 to 30 more.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 30 to the baseline as if 30 percent meant 30 extra deaths. The increase is 30 percent of 50.
15 is the increase alone. The question asks for the total in the insufficiently active group.
60 is the lower end, from the 20 percent increase. The question asks for the highest.

questions.prompt: The bone cell that breaks bone down is called an ___.
hints: The two bone cells have opposite jobs, and the other one is the osteoblast, which forms bone.
The cell asked for is the one found on bone surfaces that carries out resorption.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: osteoclast

questions.onCorrect: Osteoclasts are found on bone surfaces and are multinucleated, and they continually break down old bone.

misconceptions.feedback: An osteoblast forms new bone, so it does the opposite of what the question asks.

questions.prompt: A person's arm muscle has increased in mass and bulk, a change the textbook calls hypertrophy. What has changed inside the muscle?
hints: Recall which part of a muscle is fixed in number and which part varies.
Strength is directly related to the amount of myofibrils and sarcomeres within each fibre.

acceptedIdeas: Each fibre holds more myofibrils and sarcomeres, with the same number of fibres
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each fibre holds more myofibrils and sarcomeres, with the same number of fibres

questions.onCorrect: Hypertrophy adds contracting machinery to each fibre, and atrophy removes it, so the same fibres can be larger or smaller.

The textbook locates hypertrophy in more sarcomeres and myofibrils within the fibres, not in fluid.

questions.prompt: Which statement fits the textbook's account of the heart's four chambers?
hints: Think of an atrium as the room blood arrives in and a ventricle as the chamber that sends it on.
The textbook calls the ventricles the primary pumping chambers.

acceptedIdeas: The upper chambers receive blood and push it into the lower chambers, which pump it out
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The upper chambers receive blood and push it into the lower chambers, which pump it out

questions.onCorrect: Each side of the heart has a receiving chamber above a pumping chamber, which makes four chambers in all.

misconceptions.feedback: The roles are reversed. The atria are the upper receiving chambers, and the ventricles are the lower pumping chambers.

The upper chambers receive blood and push it into the lower chambers, which pump it out

Only the left side has an atrium and a ventricle, and the right side is a single chamber

questions.prompt: Blood has just come back from the body into the right atrium. Which chamber does it enter next, and which circuit does it then travel?
hints: The right atrium pumps blood into the chamber below it on the same side.

The left atrium, and then the pulmonary circuit through the lungs
The right ventricle, and then the systemic circuit through the body

questions.prompt: Why does the working divide 5,250 by 1,000 at the end?

Heart rate is counted per second and has to be converted to a minute
Millilitres are converted to litres, because a litre is 1,000 millilitres

Consider which of the three uses never stops.

acceptedIdeas: The basic functions of the organs
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The basic functions of the organs

choices.label: Physical activity such as exercise
Keeping the body temperature steady
The basic functions of the organs

questions.onCorrect: About 70 percent goes to the basic functions of the organs, which go on at rest.

misconceptions.feedback: Physical activity takes about 20 percent of the day's energy, which is not the largest of the three shares.
Temperature control takes about 10 percent, the smallest of the three shares.

questions.prompt: Why must the three parts of the split add up to 2,500 Calories?
hints: Add the three percentages together.
A whole day's energy use is 100 percent of itself.

acceptedIdeas: The shares of 70, 20 and 10 percent make up the whole
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The shares of 70, 20 and 10 percent make up the whole

choices.label: The shares of 70, 20 and 10 percent make up the whole
The person must eat exactly 2,500 Calories a day
The three parts are always the same size as each other

questions.onCorrect: Seventy, 20 and 10 percent together are 100 percent, so the parts must sum to the total.

misconceptions.feedback: The split describes energy used and not energy eaten, and the two need not be equal.
The three uses take very different shares of the day, so they are not equal.

questions.prompt: A person uses 2,200 Calories in a day. About 20 percent goes to physical activity. How many Calories is that?
hints: Twenty percent means 20 out of every 100, which is 0.20 as a decimal.
Multiply the day's total by that decimal.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 20 percent is 0.20, and 0.20 × 2,200 = 440 Calories.

questions.onCorrect: Physical activity takes about 440 of the 2,200 Calories, and the other two uses take the rest.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the 70 percent share, which goes to the basic functions of the organs.
That is the 10 percent share, which goes to temperature control.
That is 2 percent. Twenty percent is 0.20 of the total.

extracts.text: About 70 percent of all daily energy expenditure comes from the basic functions of the organs in the body. Another 20 percent comes from physical activity, and the remaining 10 percent is necessary for body thermoregulation or temperature control.
extracts.who: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, Chapter 24: Metabolism and Nutrition
extracts.kind: A college textbook, freely available online

questions.prompt: The WHO says free sugars should provide less than 10 percent of total daily energy intake. On a day of 2,000 Calories, how many Calories is 10 percent?
hints: Ten percent means one part in ten of the day's energy.
Multiply the total by 0.10, or divide it by 10.
Work out 2,000 ÷ 10.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 10 percent is 0.10, and 0.10 × 2,000 = 200 Calories.

questions.onCorrect: The WHO links this limit to about 50 g of free sugars for a person eating about 2,000 Calories.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 1 percent. Ten percent is one tenth of 2,000.
That is what remains after taking the 10 percent away, and the question asks for the 10 percent itself.
That is the WHO's example in grams. The question asks for Calories.

questions.prompt: An invented ready meal has 2.4 grams of salt in each portion. The WHO says adults should take in less than 5 grams of salt a day. If this meal were the only source of salt, how many whole portions stay below the limit?
hints: Find how many times 2.4 grams fits into 5 grams.
Only whole portions count, so the answer is a whole number.
Check your answer by multiplying it by 2.4 and comparing the result with 5.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 5 ÷ 2.4 is about 2.08, so two whole portions give 4.8 grams, which is below 5, and three give 7.2 grams, which is over.

questions.onCorrect: Two portions give 4.8 grams, so a single dish like this could use up nearly the whole day's allowance.

misconceptions.feedback: Three portions would give 7.2 grams of salt, which is over the 5 gram limit.
That is the exact quotient. The question asks for whole portions.

questions.prompt: Four descriptions of a way of eating are given. Which of the WHO's four principles does each one show?
hints: Look for the key idea in each description: enough, matched, limited or varied.
Balance is the only principle about energy in against energy out.
questions.onCorrect: The principles apply together, so one way of eating can show several of them at once.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Meeting needs without exceeding them is adequacy, matching energy in to energy used is balance, limiting harmful foods is moderation, and a wide variety of foods is diversity.

items.label: A week of meals that supplies every nutrient needed without going beyond need
items.explanation: Meeting nutrient needs without exceeding them, so that deficiencies are prevented, is adequacy.

items.label: Someone whose energy eaten matches the energy they use
items.explanation: Energy intake that matches energy expenditure is balance.

items.label: A diet that keeps foods that may harm health to a small share
items.explanation: Limiting foods and nutrients that may be detrimental to health is moderation.

items.label: A plate that draws on many different nutritious foods from several food groups
items.explanation: A wide variety of nutritious foods within and across food groups is diversity.

questions.prompt: On an invented day, a person uses 1,600 Calories, and about 70 percent goes to the basic functions of the organs. How many Calories is that?
hints: Seventy percent is 0.70 as a decimal.

That is the 10 percent share for temperature control.

questions.prompt: Put the path of urine in order, from the first step in the kidney to the last.
hints: Start with the structure that does the filtering, then follow the urine as it travels.
Two steps happen inside the kidney, one in the tubes, one in storage, and the last at the exit.
questions.onCorrect: MedlinePlus describes the same path: nephrons filter, the urine flows through the ureters, and the bladder stores it until you go to the bathroom.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The nephrons filter the blood, wastes and extra water become urine, the urine flows down the ureters, the bladder stores it, and it leaves the body.

items: Nephrons filter the blood
Wastes and extra water become urine
Urine flows through the ureters
The bladder stores the urine
Urine leaves the body

questions.prompt: In a male the kidneys filter about 180 litres of fluid out of the blood in a day. About how much of that leaves the body as urine?
hints: Think about what would happen to the body's water if most of 180 litres left each day.
Filtering is only the first stage. Something has to happen to the filtrate afterwards.
questions.onCorrect: The textbook gives 1 to 2 litres of urine a day, because about 99 percent of the filtrate is returned to the circulation.

choices.label: About 180 litres, which is all of it
About 90 litres, which is half of it
About 18 litres, which is a tenth
About 1 to 2 litres, a small part

acceptedIdeas: About 1 to 2 litres, a small part
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 1 to 2 litres, a small part

misconceptions.feedback: If all 180 litres left as urine, nothing would go back to the blood. The kidneys filter and then take nearly all of it back.
Half would still be far more than the kidneys let go. Reabsorption returns almost all of the filtrate.
A tenth is still too much. Only a very small share of the filtrate is left once reabsorption has done its work.

questions.prompt: Why is 1 percent of the 180 litres taken to find the urine?
hints: Ask what happens to the filtrate before it reaches the bladder.
Decide whether 1 percent is the part that goes back or the part that is left.
questions.onCorrect: Urine is what remains after reabsorption, so 99 percent returned means 1 percent left.

choices.label: Reabsorption returns only 1 percent to the blood
The bladder can hold only 1 percent of it
About 99 percent of the filtrate is reabsorbed

acceptedIdeas: About 99 percent of the filtrate is reabsorbed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 99 percent of the filtrate is reabsorbed

misconceptions.feedback: It is the other way round: 99 percent goes back to the blood and 1 percent is left to leave as urine.
The 1 percent comes from reabsorption in the nephrons, and the bladder has no part in the sum.

questions.prompt: A woman's kidneys form about 150 litres of filtrate a day and 99 percent is reabsorbed. How many litres of urine is that?
hints: Work out what share of the filtrate is not reabsorbed.
One percent is one hundredth, so divide the filtrate by 100.
150 ÷ 100 is the volume of urine in litres.
questions.onCorrect: The answer sits inside the usual 1 to 2 litres a day.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 1 percent of 150 litres is 0.01 × 150 = 1.5 litres. Using 151.2 litres gives 1.512 litres, which rounds to the same answer.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the 99 percent that went back to the blood. Urine is the 1 percent left over.
That is 10 percent of 150. Only 1 percent is left.

questions.prompt: After a person drinks a large amount of water, less ADH is released. What happens in the collecting ducts?
hints: ADH puts water channels into the duct wall. What happens to the channels when ADH falls?
If less water is recovered, is the water left in the urine, or is it taken out?
questions.onCorrect: By altering the number of channels, ADH alters how much water is recovered or lost, which also regulates blood pressure.

choices.label: Fewer channels open, more water is lost, and the urine is dilute
More channels open, more water is recovered, and the urine is concentrated
The same channels open, the same water is recovered, and the urine is unchanged
Fewer channels open, less water is recovered, and the urine is concentrated

acceptedIdeas: Fewer channels open, more water is lost, and the urine is dilute
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Fewer channels open, more water is lost, and the urine is dilute

misconceptions.feedback: That is what more ADH does. Less ADH means fewer channels, so the effect runs the other way.
ADH changes the number of water channels, so the amount of water recovered does change with it.
Fewer channels does mean less water recovered, but that water stays in the urine and makes it dilute.

questions.prompt: A person's kidneys make much less of this hormone than usual. Which body process would the passage lead you to expect to be affected?
hints: Find the hormone's name in the passage and read what it is said to stimulate.
The passage names the process in the same sentence as erythropoietin.
questions.onCorrect: Besides cleansing the blood, the kidneys regulate pH and blood pressure, and finish activating vitamin D.

choices.label: The digestion of fats in the gut
The making of red blood cells
The speed of nerve signals
The beat of the heart

misconceptions.feedback: The passage links the hormone to red blood cells, and fat digestion is not mentioned in it.
Nothing in the passage connects the kidney hormone to nerve signalling.
The passage names red blood cell production as the process the hormone stimulates, not the heartbeat.

extracts.text: Eighty-five percent of the erythropoietin (EPO) produced to stimulate red blood cell production is produced in the kidneys. The kidneys also perform the final synthesis step of vitamin D production, converting calcidiol to calcitriol, the active form of vitamin D.
extracts.who: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, Chapter 25: The Urinary System

questions.prompt: For the arithmetic only, suppose reabsorption fell from 99 percent to 98 percent while the filtrate stayed at 180 litres a day. How many litres of urine would be left?
hints: Work out what percentage is left when 98 percent is reabsorbed.
Two percent is two hundredths of 180 litres.
Divide 180 by 100 to find 1 percent, then double it.
questions.onCorrect: One percentage point of reabsorption changes the urine volume by a factor of two, because the share left over is so small.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 98 percent reabsorbed leaves 2 percent: 0.02 × 180 = 3.6 litres.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the urine at 99 percent reabsorption. At 98 percent, 2 percent is left.
That is the 98 percent that goes back. The urine is the 2 percent left over.

questions.prompt: A glomerular filtration rate of 110 mL a minute continues for a whole day of 1,440 minutes. How many litres of filtrate is that?
hints: Multiply the rate by the number of minutes in a day.
The product comes out in millilitres. There are 1,000 mL in a litre.
Divide 158,400 mL by 1,000 to convert it to litres.
questions.onCorrect: This falls between the textbook's 150 and 180 litres a day for females and males.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 110 × 1,440 = 158,400 mL, and dividing by 1,000 gives 158.4 litres.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the answer in millilitres. Divide by 1,000 to get litres.
That is 1 percent of the filtrate, which is the urine. The question asks for the filtrate.

questions.prompt: The cells lining a person's collecting ducts carry more water channels than usual. What would you expect of the urine?
hints: Water leaves the duct through the channels. Do more channels mean more or less water leaving?
Water taken out of the duct leaves the urine behind with less water in it.
questions.onCorrect: The same logic runs in reverse: with less ADH, fewer channels, less water recovered and dilute urine.

choices.label: It is more dilute, because more water is recovered
It is concentrated, because less water is recovered
It is unchanged, because channels act on filtration
It is concentrated, because more water is recovered

acceptedIdeas: It is concentrated, because more water is recovered
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is concentrated, because more water is recovered

misconceptions.feedback: More water recovered leaves less water in the urine, which makes it more concentrated, not more dilute.
More channels let more water leave the duct, so the water recovered goes up, not down.
The channels sit in the collecting ducts and act on reabsorption of water, not on filtration.

questions.prompt: Using only this summary, which person has a listed risk factor for kidney disease?
hints: Find the sentence in the summary that names what raises the risk, and list its three parts.

questions.prompt: A membrane starts at −70 mV and rises to a peak of +30 mV. By how many millivolts does the voltage rise?
hints: Sketch the number line from −70 up to +30 and mark zero.
The distance from −70 to 0 is one piece and the distance from 0 to +30 is another.
Add the two pieces together.
questions.onCorrect: The same 100 mV swing, in reverse, is the fall during repolarisation.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: From −70 to 0 is 70 mV, and from 0 to +30 is another 30 mV, so the rise is 70 + 30 = 100 mV. Equivalently, 30 − (−70) = 100.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats −70 as if it were +70 and subtracts. The start is below zero, so the climb to zero is 70 mV before the further 30 mV.
That is only the part of the rise above zero. The rise begins at −70 mV, 70 mV below zero.
That is the climb from −70 mV to zero. The rise continues on to +30 mV.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The action potential arrives, calcium channels open, vesicles release neurotransmitter into the cleft, and the neurotransmitter binds receptors on the next cell.

Neurotransmitter binds receptors on the next cell

At the receptor in the skin

hints: The arc runs input, then processing, then output.

questions.onCorrect: Sensory input, central processing and motor output are the three parts of any reflex arc.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The stimulus acts on a receptor, the signal reaches a synapse in the spinal cord, a ventral motor neuron is activated, and the biceps contracts.

questions.prompt: Put the chain the textbook describes in order, from age-related loss of smell to a higher cardiovascular risk.

questions.prompt: On a voltage trace the membrane potential moves from +30 mV back toward −70 mV. Which process is that, and which ion mainly leaves the cell?
hints: Is the voltage moving toward zero or back toward its resting value?

choices.label: Depolarisation, with sodium entering
Repolarisation, with sodium entering
Depolarisation, with potassium leaving
Repolarisation, with potassium leaving

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Repolarisation, with potassium leaving

misconceptions.feedback: That describes the rise. The fall from +30 mV back toward rest is the opposite process.
Repolarisation is the right name, but sodium entering would push the voltage up. Positive charge has to leave.
Potassium does leave, but the fall back toward −70 mV is repolarisation. Depolarisation is the rise.

questions.prompt: During depolarisation the membrane potential climbs from −70 mV, passes zero, and peaks at +30 mV. How many millivolts of the climb are above zero?

misconceptions.feedback: That is the part below zero, from −70 mV up to zero.

items.label: The membrane voltage reaches about +30 mV

items.label: Vesicles release molecules into the synaptic cleft

questions.prompt: A hormone travels in the blood past every cell in the body. Why do only some of those cells respond to it?
