hints: A low level needs glucose added to the blood.
Insulin lowers the level and glucagon raises it.
questions.onCorrect: The two hormones act as a pair, one for each direction of error.

choices.label: Insulin, which stimulates body cells to remove glucose from the blood
Glucagon, which stimulates body cells to remove glucose from the blood
Insulin, which stimulates body cells to release glucose into the blood
Glucagon, which stimulates body cells to release glucose into the blood

acceptedIdeas: Glucagon, which stimulates body cells to release glucose into the blood
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Glucagon, which stimulates body cells to release glucose into the blood

misconceptions.feedback: That is the response to a level above the range. Below it, glucose has to be added to the blood.
Glucagon is the right hormone, but it raises glucose. Removing it would lower the level further.
Releasing glucose is right for a low level, but that is the work of glucagon.

questions.prompt: Two graphs show how strong the immune response is over time after the same pathogen. One curve rises late to a low peak, and the other rises early to a high peak. Which curve belongs to the second exposure?
hints: Remember what the textbook says about a response on re-exposure.
Stronger means a higher peak and faster means an earlier rise.
questions.onCorrect: A second exposure gives a stronger and faster response, which is the basis of immunological memory.

choices.label: The one that rises late to a low peak
Neither, since they show two pathogens
The one that rises early to a high peak
Both, since the response repeats exactly

acceptedIdeas: The one that rises early to a high peak
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The one that rises early to a high peak

misconceptions.feedback: A slow, low response is what a first exposure looks like, when the adaptive response is still developing.
The curves are for the same pathogen. The difference between them is whether it is the first or the second meeting.
The textbook says the secondary response is stronger and faster than the primary one, so the two curves differ.

questions.prompt: A person meets the same pathogen for a second time and has no symptoms at all. What best explains this?
hints: Think about which response is stronger and faster on re-exposure.
Without symptoms there is no disease.
questions.onCorrect: Early exposure to pathogens spares a person from some of the same diseases later in life.

choices.label: The innate response alone is fast enough to stop it
The pathogen has become weaker since the first time
The secondary response clears it before symptoms appear

acceptedIdeas: The secondary response clears it before symptoms appear
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The secondary response clears it before symptoms appear

misconceptions.feedback: The innate response is rapid but nonspecific. The textbook credits the stronger, faster secondary adaptive response.
Nothing in the textbook says that. The explanation lies in the immune system's memory of the pathogen.

questions.prompt: Which of these describes a vaccine?
hints: The textbook's definition opens by saying what the vaccine is made from.
Which option leaves the body to build its own memory?
questions.onCorrect: The aim is immunological memory without causing much in the way of symptoms.

choices.label: A dose of antibodies made by another person
A drug that kills the pathogen directly
A cream that blocks infection on the skin
A killed or weakened pathogen, or its parts

acceptedIdeas: A killed or weakened pathogen, or its parts
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A killed or weakened pathogen, or its parts

misconceptions.feedback: A vaccine does not hand over finished antibodies. It leads the body to build its own immunological memory.
A vaccine does not attack the pathogen itself. It works through the body's own immune response.
A vaccine is not a barrier. It acts through the adaptive immune response.

questions.prompt: According to this passage, why might one year's flu vaccine not protect against the flu of the next?
hints: Look for what the passage says continuously changes.
The word that names the change is in the first sentence.
questions.onCorrect: That is why new vaccine formulations are made for each flu season.

choices.label: The virus's surface molecules change enough each year
The body forgets its memory of all viruses after a year
The adaptive response stops working for a season

acceptedIdeas: The virus's surface molecules change enough each year
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The virus's surface molecules change enough each year

misconceptions.feedback: The passage gives mutation of the virus as the reason, not the loss of memory in the body.
The passage places the change in the virus, not in the adaptive response.

extracts.text: Because viruses’ surface molecules mutate continuously, viruses like influenza change enough each year that the flu vaccine for one year may not protect against the flu common to the next. New vaccine formulations must be derived for each flu season.
extracts.who: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, Chapter 21: The Lymphatic and Immune System

questions.prompt: Why is 84 subtracted from 100 to find the children who had not had a first dose?
hints: Ask what the 84 percent counts.
All the children together make 100 percent.
questions.onCorrect: Coverage and its remainder always add up to the whole group.

choices.label: The 84 is the share who did have a dose
The 84 percent counts the children with no dose
The share with and without a dose must add to 84

acceptedIdeas: The 84 is the share who did have a dose
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The 84 is the share who did have a dose

misconceptions.feedback: The figure of 84 percent counts the children who did have a dose. The ones who did not are the rest.
It is the share who had a dose and the share who did not that add to 100 percent.

questions.prompt: In a district of 2,000 children, 84 percent had a first dose of measles vaccine. How many children is that?
hints: Write 84 percent as a decimal.
84 percent is 84 hundredths, 0.84.
Multiply 0.84 by 2,000.
questions.onCorrect: The 320 left over is the same group, seen from the other side.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 84 percent of 2,000 is 0.84 × 2,000 = 1,680 children.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number who did not have a dose, 16 percent of 2,000. The question asks for those who did.
That is 8.4 percent of 2,000. Move the decimal point one place less: 84 percent is 0.84.

questions.prompt: A headline says 'Measles vaccination is at 84 percent.' Which details do you need before you can use that number?
hints: The WHO figure named the dose, the age and the year.
A percentage needs to be of something.
questions.onCorrect: WHO reports 84 percent for one dose by the second birthday at the end of 2025, and 77 percent for two doses.

choices.label: Nothing more, since 84 percent covers every vaccine and every place
The name of the clinic that gave each of the doses
Which dose, which children, and which year it describes
Only whether the vaccine was killed or weakened

acceptedIdeas: Which dose, which children, and which year it describes
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Which dose, which children, and which year it describes

misconceptions.feedback: A coverage figure is reported for a particular vaccine and group, so it cannot be applied to every vaccine and every place.
The clinic does not change what the figure means. The dose, the children and the year do.
That describes how the vaccine is made. It does not say what the figure counts.

questions.prompt: Sort each feature into the response it describes.
hints: Ask whether the feature is about speed and generality or about specificity and memory.
Antibodies belong to B cells.
questions.onCorrect: The two responses overlap, with the innate one acting first and the adaptive one adding specificity and memory.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Rapid and nonspecific, not always effective, and quick on a new pathogen are innate. Slower at first, highly specific, B cells and antibodies, and a stronger second response are adaptive.

items.label: Rapid but nonspecific
items.explanation: The innate response is relatively rapid but nonspecific.

items.label: Not always effective, because it does not single out a pathogen
items.explanation: Being nonspecific, the innate response is not always effective.

items.label: Relatively quick to act on a new pathogen
items.explanation: It does not have to wait for the adaptive response to develop.

items.label: Slower to develop during a first infection
items.explanation: The adaptive response takes longer to develop at first.

items.label: Highly specific to a pathogen's antigens
items.explanation: Specificity is the strength of the adaptive response.

items.label: Uses B cells to make antibodies
items.explanation: B cells make antibodies, which bind specific antigens.

items.label: Gives a stronger, faster second response
items.explanation: The secondary adaptive response is the basis of immunological memory.

questions.prompt: A vaccinated person later meets the pathogen the vaccine was made against. Compared with the antibody curve of a first exposure without a vaccine, what would you expect?
hints: A vaccine leads to immunological memory.
Memory shows up as the secondary response on the graph.
questions.onCorrect: The vaccine supplies a mild first meeting, so the real pathogen meets the secondary response.

choices.label: The curve rises later and lower, because the vaccine used up the response
The curve rises earlier and higher, because memory was built
The curve is identical, because a vaccine builds no memory
The curve rises earlier but only as high as the first

acceptedIdeas: The curve rises earlier and higher, because memory was built
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The curve rises earlier and higher, because memory was built

misconceptions.feedback: A vaccine builds memory and does not use up the response, so the later meeting looks like a secondary response.
A vaccine leads to the development of immunological memory, so the curve is not identical.
The secondary response is stronger as well as faster, so the peak is higher too.

questions.prompt: WHO reports that 84 percent of children had received one dose of measles-containing vaccine by their second birthday. Out of 1,000 children, how many had not?
hints: First find the percentage who had not had a dose.
Subtract 84 from 100, then take that percentage of 1,000.
16 percent of 1,000 is 0.16 times 1,000.
questions.onCorrect: Reading what a figure leaves out is as useful as reading the figure itself.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 100 − 84 = 16 percent had not, and 16 percent of 1,000 is 0.16 × 1,000 = 160 children.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number who did have a dose, 84 percent of 1,000. The question asks for the others.
That is the percentage, not the number of children. Take 16 percent of 1,000.

flashcards.front: Which tissue is excitable and carries electrochemical signals as nerve impulses?
flashcards.back: Nervous tissue carries nerve impulses between different regions of the body.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: nervous

flashcards.front: What is the word for a tumour that poses no threat to the tissues around it?
flashcards.back: A benign tumour poses no threat to surrounding tissues, while a malignant one is capable of damage.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: benign

flashcards.front: Name the two kinds of signal that the cell's control system gives a dividing cell, and say what happens if control is lost.
flashcards.back: The system gives stop and advance signals, and loss of cell cycle control can lead to cancer.

flashcards.front: Which part of the brain works as the body's thermostat?
flashcards.back: The hypothalamus compares core temperature with its set value and starts responses that raise or lower it.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: hypothalamus

flashcards.front: What are the receptors called that report blood pressure by how much they are stretched?
flashcards.back: Baroreceptors fire faster as pressure rises and more slowly as it falls.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: baroreceptors

flashcards.front: Say what homeostasis is, and whether a value held in homeostasis stays at a single number.
flashcards.back: Homeostasis is a dynamic balance within limits compatible with life, so a value moves about inside a range.

flashcards.front: The bone cell that forms new bone is called an ___.
flashcards.back: Osteoblasts continually form new bone while osteoclasts break old bone down.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: osteoblast

flashcards.front: In muscle contraction, myosin pulls on which protein?
flashcards.back: Myosin pulls on actin once calcium has exposed the binding sites, and the process needs ATP.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: actin

flashcards.front: A baseline risk is 20 in 1,000 and the risk is 30 percent higher in another group. How many per 1,000 in that group?
flashcards.back: 30 percent of 20 is 6, and 20 + 6 = 26.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 30 percent of 20 is 6, and 20 + 6 = 26.

flashcards.front: State the number of chambers in the human heart.
flashcards.back: Two atria receive blood and two ventricles pump it out, one of each on each side.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two atria receive blood and two ventricles pump it out, one of each on each side.

flashcards.front: Cardiac output is stroke volume multiplied by what?
flashcards.back: Cardiac output is stroke volume multiplied by heart rate, in beats per minute.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: heart rate

flashcards.front: Below what resting heart rate, in beats per minute, is a rate called bradycardia?
flashcards.back: A resting rate below 60 beats per minute is bradycardia, and above 100 is tachycardia.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A resting rate below 60 beats per minute is bradycardia, and above 100 is tachycardia.

flashcards.front: What is the first, higher number of a blood pressure reading called?
flashcards.back: The first number is the systolic pressure, measured as the ventricles contract.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The first number is the systolic pressure, measured as the ventricles contract.

flashcards.front: Which vessels are the tiny ones where nutrients and wastes are exchanged?
flashcards.back: The capillaries are the tiny vessels where nutrients and wastes are exchanged.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The capillaries are the tiny vessels where nutrients and wastes are exchanged.

flashcards.front: At what reading does the NHS usually consider blood pressure high when it is checked at home?
flashcards.back: The NHS home line is 135/85 or higher, lower than its clinic line of 140/90.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The NHS home line is 135/85 or higher, lower than its clinic line of 140/90.

flashcards.front: What is the thin barrier called that is formed by the alveolar wall and the capillary wall?
flashcards.back: The alveolar and capillary walls together form the respiratory membrane, about 0.5 micrometres thick.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The alveolar and capillary walls together form the respiratory membrane, about 0.5 micrometres thick.

flashcards.front: What range of breaths a minute does the textbook give for adolescents and adults?
flashcards.back: The textbook range for adolescents and adults is 12 to 18 breaths a minute.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The textbook range for adolescents and adults is 12 to 18 breaths a minute.

flashcards.front: Why does a normal breath out need no muscular effort?
flashcards.back: The elastic lungs recoil as the diaphragm and rib muscles relax, which raises the pressure in the lungs above atmospheric pressure.

flashcards.front: What is the name for the waves of contraction and relaxation that move food along the canal?
flashcards.back: Peristalsis is the sequence of alternating waves of contraction and relaxation that propels food and helps mix it.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Peristalsis is the sequence of alternating waves of contraction and relaxation that propels food and helps mix it.

flashcards.front: Which enzyme digests the milk sugar lactose?
flashcards.back: Lactase digests lactose, and too little of it leads to lactose intolerance.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Lactase digests lactose, and too little of it leads to lactose intolerance.

flashcards.front: What is the mixture of food and digestive juices released from the stomach called?
flashcards.back: Chyme is food mixed with digestive juices, released to the small intestine in small amounts.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Chyme is food mixed with digestive juices, released to the small intestine in small amounts.

flashcards.front: Which WHO principle says that the energy taken in should match the energy used?
flashcards.back: Balance means that total energy intake matches energy expenditure.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Balance means that total energy intake matches energy expenditure.

flashcards.front: About what percentage of daily energy expenditure goes to the basic functions of the organs?
flashcards.back: About 70 percent of daily energy goes to the basic functions of the organs.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: About 70 percent of daily energy goes to the basic functions of the organs.

flashcards.front: According to the WHO, adults should take in less than how many grams of salt a day?
flashcards.back: The WHO says adults should keep salt below 5 grams a day, which is 2 grams of sodium.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The WHO says adults should keep salt below 5 grams a day, which is 2 grams of sodium.

flashcards.front: About what percentage of the filtrate is reabsorbed?
flashcards.back: About 99 percent returns to the blood, which leaves 1 to 2 litres of urine a day.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: About 99 percent.

flashcards.front: What do ADH-stimulated cells insert into the membrane of the collecting duct so that water can be recovered?
flashcards.back: Aquaporins, which are water channels, and more of them means more water recovered and more concentrated urine.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: aquaporin

flashcards.front: The tiny structures inside each kidney that filter the blood are called ___.
flashcards.back: Nephrons, of which each kidney has about a million.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: nephron

flashcards.front: The change of a stimulus into a change in membrane potential is called ___.
flashcards.back: Transduction, which is how a receptor cell turns a stimulus into a signal.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: transduction

flashcards.front: What is the resting potential of a nerve cell membrane, in millivolts?
flashcards.back: About −70 mV, with the inside negative relative to the outside.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: About −70 mV.

flashcards.front: Which ion mainly leaves the cell during repolarisation?
flashcards.back: Potassium, whose exit carries positive charge out and returns the voltage toward −70 mV.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: potassium

flashcards.front: Insulin is released when blood glucose rises above the range. Which hormone is released when it falls below?
flashcards.back: Glucagon, which stimulates body cells to release glucose into the blood.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: glucagon

flashcards.front: Type 2 diabetes accounts for approximately what percentage of all cases of diabetes?
flashcards.back: About 95 percent.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: About 95 percent.

flashcards.front: Why do thirst and frequent urination follow when blood glucose stays high?
flashcards.back: The kidneys filter the extra glucose, it draws water into the urine, and the body loses water.

flashcards.front: A protein made by B cells that binds a specific antigen is an ___.
flashcards.back: An antibody, which is secreted in a soluble form by activated B cells called plasma cells.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: antibody

flashcards.front: Which response is slower to develop in a first infection but highly specific: innate or adaptive?
flashcards.back: The adaptive response, which also gives the stronger, faster second response.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: adaptive

flashcards.front: Which three details does a coverage figure need before it can be compared with another?
flashcards.back: Which dose, which group of people and which year. Without them two figures may not describe the same thing.
